Page 1.
Salutations to the illustrious Gurus.
This is the Yoga-pāda, the supreme among all knowledge.
Salutation to Śiva and to Śakti, to the Bindu and to the Eternal One;
and to the Guru, to Gaṇeśa, and to the wise Kārttikeya. || 1 ||
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the yoga praised by those endowed with mantras;
[it belongs] to one who is peaceful, whose food and recreation are regulated, and whose exertion in actions is disciplined.
The nature of awakening from a dream has been explained; now listen to it in its true essence, O Six-faced One. || 3 ||
For one who has mastered meditation, that meditation and that fortitude serve no further purpose;
he who understands all these is fit to apply himself to yoga.
The self is the meditator, the mind is the meditation, and the subtle Maheśvara is the object of meditation;
that which is beyond this is supreme sovereignty—this is the purpose of meditation.
Having made honor and dishonor equal, and likewise pleasure and pain the same,
one who abandons joy, fear, and despondency should practice yoga with truth.
In an empty house, in a delightful monastery, in an auspicious temple, on a riverbank, in a secluded place, in a house, or even in a fearsome forest.
In a place that is secluded, solitary, silent, and devoid of people;
free from the defects of yoga, beyond conceptual construction, and without heat.
Having bathed, having touched pure water, and having bowed his head to Śiva,
and having paid homage to the teacher of yoga, he should practice yoga.
One should likewise arrange the lotus, the svastika, the upasthāpyā,
the añjali, the half-seat, the half-moon, or the bhadra, according to the ritual requirements.
Having assumed a beautiful posture with the upper body erect and the head held level,
and having abandoned all attachments, one should place the mind within the cave of the self. (11)
One should not touch the teeth with the teeth, nor the lips with the tongue;
with the eyes slightly contracted, one should properly recite the name of Śiva.
Furthermore, O Six-faced One, he is possessed of weapons that cause destruction.
His heart is not separate, nor his head, nor the cavity of his crest-lock;
his armor, weapons, and eyes proceed from that very same source.
Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal as they move within the suṣumnā, the wise one should restrain their movement and meditate upon Śiva as the Self. || 15 ||

The wise man [should perceive] that which is conjoined with inseparable connection, whose form is light, perfectly stainless, extremely subtle, all-pervading, eternal, and always free from conceptual construction. 16.
Associations are remembered as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and dull;
one should perform those breath-controls consisting of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
One should burn away the defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and it is said that concentration (dhāraṇā) is superior to that.
Breath-restraint is of three kinds: exhaling, inhaling, and filling the body. (18)
Having closed all the openings [of the body] and being devoid of inhalation and exhalation, one should remain like a completely filled jar; this is the *kumbhaka* breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). 19.
Thereafter, one should exhale the breath slowly, joined with a gentle release;
this is known as *recaka*, which can cause danger to life. || 20 ||
Having extended the forehand and placed the knee [on the ground] while circumambulating to the right, one should then snap the fingers; this is declared to be the "desired" (naiṣṭhā) mudrā. (21)
Twelve *mātrās* should be known as the measure designated as a *tāla*;
twelve *tālas* should be known as one *prāṇāyāma*, which is equal to a breath.
The middle [practice] is twenty-four [breaths], and the superior should be double that.
The best among those who know yoga should increase it by one mātrā each day. (23)
One should increase it gradually, neither too quickly nor with delay;
for it is held that the supreme *prāṇāyāma* is doubled by *dhāraṇā*.
Yoga is twice as effective as dhāraṇā, and yoga itself is doubled [in its result]; this is known as the perfection of yoga (yogasiddhi) by Śiva, the Supreme Self. || 25 ||
Then he perceives within himself the subtle element of smell, as well as taste, form, touch, and the subtle element of sound itself. (26)
Through the yoga of action, one perceives [the Self] through various states of the castes, as well as ego, mind, intellect, the qualities, the unmanifest, and the principle of the Person. (27)
One should know these as manifested from the characteristics of the qualities of one's own nature (svadharma):
first knowledge (vidyā), then the arts (kalā), then time (kāla), then illusion (māyā), and then the supreme knowledge (vidyā).
Having seen all of them in succession, one should again pierce them with the weapon-mantra;
then the principle of Vidyeśvara, and likewise the supreme Sādāśiva.
Having pierced [the subtle body] with the razor-edged weapon (kṣurikāstra), one should then enter the subtle Śiva;
for the knower of yoga, when intent upon Him, Śiva Himself becomes manifest as the nature of nectar within that [subtle body]. 30.
He is omniscient, omnipresent, subtle, the lord of all, and the creator of all;
in all scriptures indeed, this fourfold object is to be known. (31)

Having understood the true nature of the categories (tattvas) in their proper order—namely, the bound soul (paśu), the bond (pāśa), the Lord (pati), and Śiva—one attains the essence of the Tantra, which is indeed difficult to obtain. || 32 ||
Even while existing in every respect, he does not again take up a body.
Thus ends the Yoga-pāda.
I truly desire to hear the arrangement of the individual souls (paśu) and their fetters (pāśa);
likewise, O Maheśvara, tell me of their conjunction.

The fetters (pāśas) are primary; among them, the individual soul (jīva) is indeed the first. But what are the fetters said to be? Why are they called "tender" (komala)? And why is the person (pumān) bound? || 2 ||
What kind of husband is to be known as one established in the state of authority?
And what kind of Śiva is said to be devoid of authority? || 3 ||
The Self is both the Lord and the bound soul (paśu); it is independent, pure consciousness, yet defiled by the mind;
it is equally deluded, eternally transmigrating, and when possessing some knowledge, it is made into a Lord.
Just as the state of being gold exists within copper itself, though it is cut off from view;
so too should the state of being Śiva within the individual (pudgala) be understood as being internally cut off from view. || 5 ||
Just as copper, when processed with mercury, attains the state of gold, so too the self, through its connection with knowledge, attains the state of Śiva.
Just as [the butter] situated in milk is known through differentiation, so too the Self, though conjoined with bonds, remains situated in non-differentiation. (7)
Just as one removes poison through the powers of meditation,
so too does the teacher effect the severance of the bonds through the sacrifices dedicated to Śiva. (8)
Just as the suppression of poison occurs through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs,
so too does the suppression of all bonds occur through initiation (dīkṣā).
Just as the impurities of the bodily constituents (dhātus) being consumed by fire are burned away,
so too the Teacher, having become like the wind, burns away both impurities of men.
The bonds (pāśas) are known to be subordinate qualities; merit and demerit (dharmādharmau) are known as impurities (malas).
These two are innate for practitioners and those possessing knowledge, existing like copper and its blackness.
Those fetters are remembered as being threefold: innate, adventitious, and likewise those arising from association; now hear the definitive analysis concerning them.
O Guha, those principles beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātra), which are subtle and all-pervading, are declared to be the supreme fetters (pāśa) that are innate to all living beings. (13)
The sense organs and the elements have their origin in that which is their seed;
for these are known to be adventitious, and therefore they are further characterized by association.
Whatever action may arise from association, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, those bonds born of association yield the fruits of pleasure and pain. (15)
Through action, however, bodies arise; from the existence [of latent dispositions], the emergence of action occurs. The existence of previously acquired karmas is the cause of their conjunction.
The Lord may be the manifestor of these [qualities] according to the nature of their karma;
from the arising of karma, creation occurs, and they know dissolution to be caused by them. (17)
O Śikhidhvaja, through the fault of attachment to sense objects, even a person who is a non-doer and omnipresent incurs bondage by becoming attached to qualities. (18)
Just as a father is bound alone for the offense of his son, so too in this world may a man incur bondage even though he is not the doer. (19)
Just as even a neutral person incurs bondage through association with the virtuous, so too should the *pudgala* be understood. || 20 ||

The bonds are without beginning or end, while the individual soul (jīva) is proclaimed to be without beginning. Likewise, the one who severs them is without beginning; he is the Lord of Paśus and Pāśas.
He should be known as Śiva, whose nature is mantra and whose form is mantra;
he is the sovereign of all mantras and the agent of creation and dissolution. || 22 ||
He, the support of all existence, seated upon the throne of the Yoga-pīṭha, is always worshipped with [offerings] endowed with specific footprints, colors, and other attributes. (23)
Thus has Pati been fully described as the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
he is indeed of gross, subtle, and mixed form, thus purified in nature.
Beyond that is the supreme reality of Śiva, which transcends mantras, is stainless, free from affliction, without support, and devoid of the form of letters. || 25 ||
He is omniscient, omnipresent, peaceful, the self of all, and facing in every direction; he transcends the senses, is without support, exceedingly subtle, eternal, and constant.
That very Blessed One is all-pervading, immeasurable, and indeed incomparable;
he exists like oil within a sesame seed, through the division of exterior and interior.
p. 7) The Chapter on the Direct Realization of One’s Own Self.
Now, O Guha, I shall explain to you another method according to reality,
for the sake of that which is ungraspable, subtle, all-pervading, and partless.
That by which one correctly understands, and knowing which one becomes auspicious—that realization has not been declared to anyone; listen to it from me. || 2 ||
It has come down through the lineage of gurus, unseen by all the primordial beings (Ādibuddhas), for the sake of liberation from the bonds of existence; it is supreme and faces in every direction.
He who is the all-pervading deity, the self of all, whose face is turned in every direction; who consists of all reality, who is to be meditated upon, and who is established above everything. || 4 ||
Transcending all principles and devoid of speech, mind, and name—one should worship that very Self with a non-conceptualizing mind. || 5 ||

That very knowledge which is partless, eternal, constant, and imperishable; which is free from conceptual construction, beyond the reach of the mind, and devoid of logical reasons or illustrative examples.
It is without marks, imperishable, peaceful, beyond the range of sense objects, ineffable, and free from doubt; that is I—of this there is no doubt.
I alone am the supreme deity, Śiva, who consists of all mantras;
yet I transcend all mantras and am devoid of creation and dissolution.
All this—visible and invisible, moving and unmoving—is pervaded by me;
I alone am the Lord of the World, and from me everything shines forth.
The entire collection of worlds, the universe differentiated by manifold forms from Śiva down to the earth—all that is established within me. (10)
Whatever is seen or even heard in this world,
all that is pervaded by me, through the distinction of external and internal. (11)
If one worships out of delusion with the thought, "I am the self, Śiva is indeed another, the Supreme Self," one shall not attain the state of Śiva. || 12 ||
"Śiva is one and I am another"—one should abandon such a sense of separation.
One should always contemplate non-duality, thinking: "He who is Śiva, that indeed am I. (13)
One who is endowed with the contemplation of non-duality and is established in the Self everywhere perceives that which is all-pervading and resides within all bodies; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, for the yogin who abides in the state of a single self and is free from conceptual construction, omniscience comes forth.
He who is recited in all the scriptures as the unborn Lord, the bodiless and qualityless Self—that indeed am I; of this there is no doubt.
For that which is unperceived is the animal, being dependent on the law of creation;
but that which is perceived is eternal, pure, and Śiva—of this there is no doubt. || 17 ||

Therefore, the Self should always be known and thoroughly investigated by the wise, through the distinction between the higher and the lower, and according to the division of the gross and the subtle. 18.
The supreme [form] is the ultimate nirvāṇa, distinguished by its freedom from conceptual elaboration;
it is declared to be gross when consisting of mantra, and subtle when established solely in meditation. || 19 ||
Or rather, O Six-faced One, what is the use of speaking at length?
This particular elaboration of speech only causes delusion to the mind.
All phenomena do not exist; whatever one may conceptualize, that very thing comes to be without doubt, because its nature always exists as such. (21)
Thus, the knowledge of the Self has been briefly explained;
having understood that everything consists of the Self, one should worship the Self alone. (22)
Therein, neither gods, nor Vedas, nor sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees exist;
for they rely instead upon the stainless, all-encompassing self-knowledge.
For living beings submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra who seek refuge, there is no other giver of refuge anywhere at any time except for the knowledge of the Self. 24.
He who, having become supreme, knows the self in its true nature,
is liberated without effort, even while remaining in every state of existence.
There is no other gain found anywhere superior to the attainment of the Self;
therefore, one should worship this very Self, for it is the Supreme. 26.
There is neither prāṇa nor apāna, nor likewise any distinct organ;
one should always remember that Self as omniscient and perfectly complete. (27)
Neither internally nor externally, neither too far nor too near—
there, in that supreme state which is partless, he should fix his mind.
One should constantly meditate upon oneself as being entirely empty—like that appearance of darkness—extending horizontally, upwards, and downwards, both outside and inside. (29)
One should worship the Self, which is neither empty nor non-empty, and which is indeed both non-empty and empty— being entirely free from partiality.
One should worship the Self, which is free from disease, without support, devoid of color and form, stainless, and beyond all qualities. (31)
One should worship the Self, which is free from disease, without support, immeasurable, incomparable, eternally pure by nature, and permanent. 32.
Having renounced all actions, free from desire and devoid of attachment,
one should contemplate the Self by means of the self, abiding within the very Self alone.
Having abandoned these states— place, birth, and social relations, as well as those associated with caste and stage of life— the wise man should contemplate his own true nature.
This is the mantra, this indeed is the deity, this is the meditation, and this is the austerity.
Having abandoned all states of being, one should contemplate the state of the Self.
Relying on existence within non-existence, one should make existence supportless;
having established the mind in the Self, one should not think of anything at all. (36)
One should attend upon the Self, which is neither conceivable nor inconceivable, which is mindless yet is indeed the mind itself, and which is utterly free from partiality.
Having made the mind supportless, one should constantly contemplate the inconceivable;
thus, when it has become free from reality and partless, one finds that bliss which resides in the Self. (38)
That bliss which is non-conceptual, inconceivable, devoid of cause and example, is declared to be supreme, ultimate, and incomparable. (39)
Having cast off attachment to sense objects, one should abandon the fluctuations of the mind;
when it attains the state of *unmanī*, then that is supreme bliss. (40)
The practice of yoga is studied in all directions, places, and times;
and among all castes and stages of life, no difference in knowledge exists. (41)
Just as the milk of cows of many different colors is of a single color, so too one perceives the knowledge of the possessor of the body (the self) as being equal to that of the cows. (42)
Since Brahman is omnipresent, all-pervading, and faces in every direction, one should not consider directions or locations within that which is established as Brahman. || 43 ||
For one who is established in the Supreme Self, no purpose is served by ritual action, nor is any prescribed duty remembered; there is no gender, nor conduct pertaining to the stages of life.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, eating, or even drinking—at all times, at every moment, and amidst wind, cold, and heat—(he remains thus). 45.
In the midst of fear, poverty, and disease—such as lethargy, fever, and the like—he remains established within himself as peaceful; indeed, he is self-satisfied and partless.
I have not gone, nor have I gone, nor shall I go; I do not go.
I have not existed, nor will I exist, for I abide in the nature of eternal reality.
But actions are indeed natural, and nature is the source of action; therefore, one who knows the truth should think, "I do nothing at all. (48)
There is no bondage to primordial nature (prakṛti); this is called liberation.
Nor am I ever defiled by the defects of primordial nature.
Just as a lamp shines after the darkness has been dispelled,
so does the supreme Self shine forth once the heat born of ignorance has been removed.
Just as a lamp, through its oil and wick, seeks extinction by force,
so too the self, when joined with meditative cultivation, becomes firmly established within itself.
Just as when a pot containing space is being carried away,
the pot is led along while the space attains the state of space; (52)
Thus, by means of this authority, the omniscient one who possesses such authority [declared] regarding the diverse material body as well as the individual self and the supreme self. (53)
Completely liberated from all bonds, he becomes omniscient and omnipresent. || 54 ||
Then, having abandoned all discursive thoughts and grasped the pure yoga of self-concentration,
knowing that there is nothing else here beyond this, one should completely relinquish the conceptual constructions of the mind.
Having thus worshipped consciousness, the wise man, constantly disciplined, enters the bodiless state;
liberated here, he becomes all-pervading, possessing those qualities, and abiding both within and without. (56)
Omniscience, contentment, primordial awakening, sovereignty, eternal and undiminished power, infinite power, a stainless self, and a purified body—he attains the state of Śiva. 57.

There is no recitation, no worship, no bathing, no fire-offering, and no spiritual practice; there is no fruit of merit or demerit, nor is there the offering of rice-balls or the libation of water. (58)
For him there are no restrictive rules (niyamas), nor is fasting prescribed; he has neither engagement nor withdrawal, nor the vows of celibacy (brahmacarya). 59.
There is no entering into fire, nor falling from a cliff or into water;
having drunk the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva, wander at your pleasure. 60.
Like Śiva, he is eternal, pure, and devoid of the nature of creation;
truth, truth, and again truth—this triple truth is the established rule.
O Guha, there is nothing further beyond this to be known anywhere.
It purifies all states of being; it is the stainless self, the stainless intellect, and thus the pure consciousness. (62)
The pure one, through a pure state of being, perceives everything as pure:
the waking-within-waking, the waking-dream, as well as the waking-deep-sleep.
The waking state is the Turya (the Fourth), which transcends the supreme time; it is the vision of the Supreme, the cessation within the foremost of all things, and indeed the vision of Śiva.
Including "sāyujya" as a distinct category, eleven [types] are traditionally recorded above. || 65 ||
I shall further declare the supreme means of creating doubt, the most excellent method for creating doubt:
how the self is designated as the "living being" (*jīva*), and so forth.
The mantra-soul is called the supreme, and there is indeed nothing higher than that;
[so too are] earth, water, fire, air, and space.
The union of all beings is proclaimed as the self of the elements (bhūtātman),
through the seeds presided over by the Puruṣa, which are joined with the subtle elements (tanmātra) that constitute the seeds.
The great elements arise together with the subtle essence (malaya);
that which is joined with all the sense organs is called the body. || 4 ||
Its very destruction and arising are known to consist of food;
from the transformation of food, the production of the nutrient essence (rasa) will occur.

From plasma comes blood; from blood, flesh; from flesh, fat; in the fat are the bones; from the bones, marrow; from marrow, semen. Through the union of semen and blood, and through the conjunction with the vital wind (*vāyu*), the embryo is produced.
Just as [the seed] is consumed by fire... [text fragment].

(14) In that regard, the navel is in the middle of the body. At the site of the navel is impurity (*mala*). Just as wind, bile, and phlegm reside at the site of impurity—due to the collection of these three impurities—from the union during the period of menstruation, the semen of the male...
From an excess [of semen], a male is born; from an excess of the mother's blood, a female is produced;

from the equality of both, a neuter is born. Furthermore, those who are deformed—such as being blind, humpbacked, or dwarfed—are born due to mutual discordance and being afflicted by each other's vital airs (*vāyu*). From the imbalance in the union of the male and female, the semen...

It becomes of such a nature. By that, a pair is produced. After one night, it is a *kalala*; after five nights, a *budbuda* (bubble); after seven nights, a *māṃsapeśī* (flesh-mass) comes into being; after fourteen nights, it takes the form of a *māṃsapiṇḍa* (flesh-lump). Within one month, the arms and shoulders are formed; by the second month—

The thumbs, feet, and other limbs are produced. In three months, the fetal membrane (jarāyu), sinews, skin, and hide come into being. In four months, the backbone, chest, and hips are formed. In five months, the head, forehead, ears, and nose are formed. In six months, the apertures are formed.
In seven months, the manifestation of the body occurs; in eight months, the form becomes complete;

in nine months, it is endowed with consciousness. It remembers its previous birth and thinks, "I am he. It begins to move. Like a pot within another pot, it is perceived through water; due to its subtlety, it is like the blue of the sky.

For example: Therefore, consciousness is joined with the fivefold [elements]. Intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), mind (*manas*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—and from primordial nature, the person (*puruṣa*). By means of the mind, one forms a volition; indeed, being thus joined with the mind, one is then joined with the sense organs. From the sense organs, there is always [perception] regarding objects.
it proceeds.

Thus, the body, which is by nature the primordial material (prakṛti), must be set in motion by conditions (pratyaya). Because [the qualities] are non-existent [independently], they produce the differentiation of the person's (puruṣa) own nature into sattva, rajas, and tamas. || 18 ||
O Guha, the quality of passion (rajas), which is characterized by sovereignty, manifests the state of being (bhāva) that illuminates sentient beings.
Tamas produces a state characterized by delusion for embodied beings;
from sattva arises knowledge, and from rajas, indeed, confusion.
From Tamas arise untruth, ignorance, negligence, and indolence;
from Sattva arise truth, compassion, fortitude, humility, and steadfastness. (21)
From rajas arises anger and mercilessness. Those established in sattva go upward; those characterized by rajas remain in the middle.
Established in the lowest quality, those characterized by darkness (tamas) go from there; O Six-faced One, when rajas and tamas are overcome, sattva increases.
Whether it be passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), or darkness (tamas), whichever of these qualities a person is constantly attached to through excessive attachment, [that quality prevails]. (24)
Having become superior to him as well, one should employ him in his own duty;
in this way, there are sixteen side-pavilions for a single-kapāla [temple]. || 25 ||
There are three hundred [bones], nine hundred sinews, and nine gates; five *prasthas* of marrow, two *prasthas* of fat, and thirty million hairs on the upper body. (26)
There are eighty-one palas of fluid; its joint is one and two [palas]; the tongue measures twelve palas;
the rectum is five and a half palas; the semen is three kuḍavas; and the bile is one āḍhaka.
And there are seven hundred and fifty [types of beings].
It should be understood that the excretion of urine and feces is not fixed, because it depends on the nature of the food consumed.
Thus, this self of beings is called "Puruṣa";
the word that exists subsequently is the activator of its verbal expression. (29)
Through the union of prāṇa and apāna, he is proclaimed as the inner self (antarātman);
from him proceed all the scriptures, both in Sanskrit and Prakrit.
It proceeds eternally and according to rule through the local dialects and other means, as do beasts, wild animals, birds, and reptiles. (31)
Whatever beings always move swiftly,
they are indeed subtle— the five tanmātras, as well as the mind and the ego.
Intellect is to be known as eightfold; the qualities (guṇas), the unmanifest (avyakta), and that which belongs to the Person (pauruṣa);
as well as Kalā, Kāla, Māyā, Vidyā, and Vidyeśvara. (33)
Sadāśiva, as well as the Tattva, the Veda, and the end of the lineage—through the conjunction of these alone, the Puruṣa is known as the essence of the Tattvas. (34)
By these, this entire world is pervaded; and these fetters consist of impurity.
Extremely subtle, all-pervading, impermanent, innate, and present in all seasons. || 35 ||
Nature (prakṛti) must be understood, and its process (prakriyā) is explained;
there is nothing higher than knowledge of the process, nor is there anything more pervasive than Śilā.
There is no accomplishment higher than yoga, and no happiness greater than tranquility;
O Six-faced One, the arising of the reality of the sacrifice occurs within the body.
Then the embodied soul, consisting of those [eight] states, always follows after the modification; that reality in which the self of beings moves, that very reality it pursues. (38)
Having become all the principles (tattvas), that embodied soul repeatedly attains identity with them, following the sequence of all the principles. (39)
It moves about without differentiation and is always all-pervasive;
and that [pervasiveness] belongs to it, O Skanda, through its various essential natures at all times. (40)
O Six-faced One, even though it is all-pervasive, it is perceived as having arising, setting, and remaining; likewise, it grasps the entities that are the lords of the principles (tattvas). 41.
For the self consists of all phenomena; one may fashion it according to one's desire.
Whatever state in which one finds delight, that very state one cultivates. || 42 ||
One should know stability in that reality and perform each respective action.
Therefore, having understood this, the wise person should take delight in the stainless reality of Śiva, which is changeless and without support.
Furthermore, O Six-faced One, delusion does not return to that very place.
Even at this final hour, by abiding in this [state], the embodied soul shall attain the supreme emanation;
it is omnipresent, subtle, ancient, eternal, and firm.
The eternal one, who is the speaker of the essence, is the pervader of all principles;
yet he is dependent, bound, pure consciousness alone, and defiled by impurity.

One who is deluded, eternally subject to saṃsāra, possessing only limited knowledge, and inactive—his state should be known as the "dharma of the beast" (paśudharma); the "dharma of Śiva" (śivadharmas) is otherwise than that.
The source of the animal-nature of man indeed assumes many forms:
he is called the self (ātman), the creature (jantu), the person (pumān), the embodied one (dehin), the male (puruṣa), and likewise the individual (pudgala). (48)

The individual soul (jīva), the wearer of the skull (kapālī), the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and others such as Parameṣṭhin—all these exist within the virtuous-souled one, joined with all their respective functions. || 49 ||
One attains all bodies and enters into all wombs;
as long as wisdom does not arise, one wanders about due to karma.
But the ignorant one, whose body is enveloped [by ignorance] and who is overwhelmed by suffering and grief, whereas the knower, having attained the supreme peace, reaches it before long. (51)
Then, the abandonment of all sufferings arises for him.
Thus ends the section on the self as a real entity and so forth.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the Puruṣa, whose very form is mantra— blazing, the remover of all sorrow, and the supreme destroyer of all sins.
Of all the gods, asuras, and yakṣas; of the kinnaras, asuras, and rākṣasas; and of the hosts of ancestors and mothers, as well as among the siddhas, vidyādharas, and others.
The mantras and vidyās of the nāgas, gandharvas, animals, yakṣas, piśācas, humans, Śiva, and all other such beings are eternal. (3)
There is nothing whatsoever, whether stationary or moving, that exists without mantras; all sentient beings, in whatever form they may be, have their bodies empowered by mantras.
For whichever reality there may be, one should apply its first syllable, as well as the sixth and the thirteenth, to that very reality.
One should know that mantra to be the supreme essence of all reality, adorned with the *bindu* at its head, which bestows the fruit of all desires. (6)
One should employ their limbs [as mantras], for Brahmā is not proclaimed to reside within them.
Indeed, the limbs are known as long vowels separated [by consonants], joined with the *netra* (the letter *i*) and the *anusvāra*. (7)
That which is known as the Visarga is indeed the Astra-mantra, devoid of the Anusvāra;
thus, one should place a Bindu upon the head of those seed-syllables (bījas).
Mantras illuminated by the syllable Oṃ and joined with a salutation (namaḥ) at the end should be employed in worship;
in the fire-oblation (homa), they should be joined with "svāhā" at the end.
[This applies] to its invocation, its placement in the vessels, the rites of sipping water (ācamana),
the bathing, the ritual arrangement of mantras, and the acts of wearing [the ashes] and meditating.
Whatever ritual procedure for Śiva has been prescribed for the performance of worship and offerings, for the acts of recitation and fire-oblation, and for all sequences of ritual action; || 11 ||
One should apply that same procedure to all the principles whatsoever;
whatever may be unmentioned, all of that should be performed with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Thus, one who knows the procedure and is a knower of mantras should undertake the rite with discernment; this is declared to be the "supreme unification" (paramīkaraṇa) among all principles.

Just as a mantra exists through the distinction between the expressed and the expresser, so too is that person (puruṣa) known as the essence of mantra, consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme. || 14 ||
The gross [element] attains its established denotation and enters into union with the subtle;
the supreme [element], having attained which there is no returning, is the ultimate Nirvana. (15)
Just as a lamp, while being perceived, appears as many yet remains one;
so too a mantra, when being conceptualized, appears as many yet remains one. 16.
Just as in the world water, though of a single genus, appears in many different forms, so too should it be understood that a mantra, though of a single genus, possesses many different forms. (17)
Whichever mantra one seeks to accomplish, one should conceive of it as being my very self;
for its limbs are traditionally held to consist of that essence, while those placed externally are deprived of two parts.
Whatever kind of form has been chosen by whom, for that person it is exactly of that kind;
even such a ritual procedure, however, is in accordance with the mantra and the deity.
One should fashion the mantra according to its form by following the path taught in the scriptures;
having become such a form, the mantra will then accomplish the ritual action.
However, due to the various dispositions of the listener, the form of the phonemes appears in diverse ways, assuming all possible qualities like a crystal gem. (21)
Thus the Puruṣa, consisting of the Mātrās, has been described as the accomplisher of all aims;
for he is indeed omniscient, omnipresent, and composed of all forms. || 22 ||
I shall describe that which is higher than the highest, beyond mantra, stainless,
free from affliction, without support, and devoid of the form of letters.
He is omniscient, all-pervading, peaceful, the self of all, and facing in every direction; he is beyond the senses, without support, exceedingly subtle, eternal, and free from suffering.
The Supreme Self is proclaimed to be free from parts, the support of night, inexpressible, all-pervasive, eternal, devoid of suffering, and the object of valid cognition. || 25 ||
In whatever state of being a person worships [the Lord] at any time, in that very way—whether as one or as many—he attains Him. (26)
Whatever form one may contemplate, all of it exists within the Self;
for the Self, as explained in its sixfold expansion, is said to be the bestower of all desires. (27)

For he exists as the elemental self (bhūtātman), the inner self (antarātman), the essential self (tattvātman) known as the individual soul (jīva), the self of mantra (mantrātman), and the one called the supreme (paramātman); though he is but one, he is established in many ways. || 28 ||
The self of the elements (bhūtātman) arises from the conjunction of the elements; the self of the principles (tattvātman) is established in the principles;
the self of the mantra (mantrātman) is that which is to be known as the mantra; and the inner self (antarātman) is endowed with speech. || 29 ||
But the enjoyer of pleasures and pains, abiding in primordial nature (prakṛti) and endowed with the qualities (guṇas),
having conquered their own realm through these [means], becomes liberated and supreme.
One who is ever-disciplined shall indeed attain sovereignty over all forms;
yet even having attained it, that state becomes twofold, and one may undergo rebirth once more. || 31 ||
Through prior investigation and examination, the karma of sin is exhausted;
and at the time of the discernment of reality, one realizes non-duality.
For the Supreme Self is indeed one alone, yet it appears manifold due to the diversity of minds;
though one, it has many names differentiated by millions of distinct forms.
Those deluded by erroneous cognition attribute names to that which is nameless;
yet, just as stainless knowledge is manifested, it faces every direction.
Then one finds that supreme, eternal, and constant Dharma which belongs to the Self;
for it is remembered that the Self alone is the Supreme, the Puruṣa, and the Cause. || 35 ||
I alone am the Supreme Brahman; I am the object of knowledge, beyond all thought. All things that are subject to destruction are merely various modifications of the mind. (36)
Free from both existence and non-existence, I alone am the imperishable Śiva;
one whose actions have been renounced through yoga and whose doubts have been shattered by knowledge. (37)
Then, free from conceptual construction, one should constantly worship the Self,
having cast off all latent impressions, satisfied in the Self and free from affliction.
One who is endowed with the contemplation of non-duality should always worship the Self,
which is eternal, stainless, immutable, and free from all that is removed.
By means of the pervasive, subtle, supreme eye of yoga,
[one perceives that which is] pure, eternal, constant, the object of knowledge, and incomparable.
It is free from conceptual construction and inconceivable, devoid of causes and examples;
it is difficult to perceive, devoid of qualities, peaceful, transcending reality, and stainless.
I behold the Lord as my very self—indistinguishable and free from doubt;
all-pervading, residing within all bodies, omnipresent, and facing in every direction.
One beholds the auspicious Self, which is free from affliction and without support.
Let him behold the various paths of practice, the higher and lower Mantras and Tantras,
and the entire universe— both manifest and unmanifest— as present within the Self.
All-knowing and all-seeing, perfectly complete and utterly stainless,
liberated and having become the Absolute, he shall attain imperishable bliss.
Thus ends the Jñānapāda in the Sarvajñānottara.
Just as the flower is the essence of trees and the milk-ocean is the essence of all oceans,
so too is the Śiva-āgama the essence of all scriptures.
It is the means for accomplishing all branches of learning, complete with many categories of meaning. (1)
Listen now in due order to that which is concise in words yet vast in meaning:
that which is beyond the senses, ungraspable, transcending reality, and stainless.
The omniscient, all-pervading, peaceful, the self of all, and facing every direction—
from Him emerged the scripture, which is the form of sound and free from all affliction.
Having entered the extremely subtle and supreme Vaindava-tattva, which fulfills all desires, and having awakened that [disciple] for a moment, [he should proceed].
Furthermore, this subtle characteristic was obtained by me from Sadāśiva;
from that, the vowels and consonants arose, originating from the color of the *haṃsa*.
Furthermore, mantras and treatises endowed with meter and grammatical characteristics came into being;
from the supreme *nāda* (sound-vibration), articulate sound (*śabda*) is produced.
Syllables alone are known as mantras, and within the mantra reside the presiding deities;
when propitiated according to the prescribed rule, they grant all desires.
Through the conjunction of vowels and consonants, the moving and the unmoving, the visible and the invisible [are manifested];
therefore, one should cause the consonants to be perceived, preceded by the union of vowels.
Thus ends the chapter on the Origin of Mantra and Tantra in the Śrī-Sarvajñānottara.
O Śaṅkara, tell me in truth the ritual procedure for the sacrifice of the phonemes (varṇayāga), preceded by the conjunction of vowels, as well as the process of supreme unification (paramīkaraṇa).
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the sequence of the ritual procedure for the sacrifice of the letters,
beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *kṣa*, preceded by their union with the vowels.
Each single syllable is divided by the twelve vowels;
those with short vowels are designated as Brahman, while one should indicate the limbs (aṅgas) by means of the long vowels. (3)
Through their conjunction with the anusvāra, they are proclaimed as the "three-eyed" (trayonetrāḥ);
those with the visarga are remembered as the "weapons" (astrāḥ), while those devoid of the anusvāra are likewise [designated].
One should apply the seed-syllable of the heart, the fifth seed-syllable, and the sixth seed-syllable;
joined with three morae, one should place a bindu upon the head.
One should know this auspicious procedure in this manner for all castes in their proper sequence;
one may arrange the short, long, protracted, and infinite vowels according to one's desire.
One should cause death by means of the syllable *phaṭ* joined with the beginning and end of the short [mantra];
if one is possessed by wrath, one should recite it with blood-red eyes.
Combined with the syllable *hriṃ* at the end and the three long vowels, it will certainly subjugate [the target].
Having become a great practitioner (*sādhaka*), one should indeed fashion the object of practice (*sādhya*). (8)
Having emerged, one should enter by the path that has arisen;
having become non-dual while remaining there, one should draw it back again by that very same path.
One should fix the mind upon the limbs within the limbs for the sake of binding; then, one should withdraw that [mind], situated like the interior of a lotus bud, by means of the heart.
Whatever action one performs, it is not considered a reproach against the deity; one should recite that name, joined with meditative visualization, as if it were a revealed mantra. (11)
Mantras should be known as being endowed with the *bindu* (the nasal drop) and joined at the beginning with the *praṇava* (OM);
one should employ them in worship when they are likewise joined at the end with a salutation (*namaskāra*).
In rites of pacification (śāntika), attraction (ākarṣa), and nourishment (pauṣṭika), [the mantra] should be joined with "home" at the end;
and in the rite of subjugation (vaśya), it should be employed joined with the utterance of "svāhā" at the end. (13)
Or what is the use of this extremely extensive ritual of mantras?
O child, listen to the concise and detailed account that is common to all.
Whatever ritual procedure for the King of Mantras is being proclaimed, one should always apply that very same procedure to all the vowels.
In the same manner, one should employ [this] in the sacrifice to all the gods.
Thus ends the chapter on the extraction of mantras with gross phonemes in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrī-Sarvajñānottara.
I shall proclaim the extraction of the mantra according to reality; listen, O Six-faced One, for it is extremely secret, supremely subtle, and consists of all mantras. (1)

That power which, residing repeatedly within the *mātraka* and other [centers], is coiled like a snake ready to strike, is the supreme, most subtle Śakti whose nature is the manifestation of the universe. (2)
Spreading upwards in various ways, her form extended as she was impelled; like a female elephant with her trunk, she remained resting upon her chest.
That auspicious [lineage] is made very long by means of a continuous succession of great power;
through its tradition, it swiftly liberates itself.
This very one previously mentioned is she by whom that which is to be done is performed;
she reveals the self, as well as the supreme and non-supreme gateway to liberation.
A wise man should travel to the Middle Country together with that beautiful woman;
having reached the Middle Country, he should abandon that fickle woman.
Having understood the root-measure (*mūlamātra*) of power, which is exceedingly difficult to conquer in its middle state, that by which its root is produced is called the "awakener" (*bodhaka*). (7)
The manifestation of all seeds is subject to the power of utterance;
it is the long nasal resonance (nāda), indeed immeasurable and incomparable. || 8 ||
The utterance of the *prāsāda* mantra is remembered as being smooth, clear, deep, and powerful; it is joined with the sixth [vowel] and again conjoined with the end of the sixth.
Joined with the half-moon and the bindu, and adorned with the three measures (mātrās),
he is declared to be the eternal Śiva, the highest of all knowledge.
The pronunciation of that [syllable] is proclaimed by those who know the mantras after discerning the eight [components].
One should indicate the five Brahmans through their association with the short vowels. (11)

Indeed, O dear one, that Gāyatrī of great luster, whose limbs are known to be long and distinct, and whose causal self is the Bindu at the crown of the head within the mouth of the Suṣumṇā, should be pointed out.
In the beginning of the vowels, there are three long [vowels]; this is proclaimed as the triple reality (tritatva).
That should be known as the three eyes; one should apply them in their proper sequence.
One should place the Ātma-tattva on the right, the Vidyā-tattva on the left, and the Śiva-tattva on the forehead; thus, these three principles are to be distributed across the five [limbs].
The wise one, knowing the eyes, should first place the eye upon his own faces in the proper sequence, and then likewise upon those of Śiva. (15)
One should arrange the Vidyeśas as merged with the end of the thirteen [vowels];
and for the Gaṇeśas, one should employ the Gāyatrī, in which they have arrived at a state of presence.
The heart-mantra of the world-protectors should be known as that which fulfills all desires;
one should then fashion the blazing Pāśupata weapon-mantra.
(27) All are joined with the *bindu*, possessing a radiance like that of pure jasmine or the moon;
they are the creators of the universe, the knowers of the universe, the makers of the universe, and the embodiments of the universe. || 18 ||
Mantras illuminated by the syllable Oṃ and joined with a salutation at the end should be employed for worship;
in the fire-oblation (homa), they should be combined with "svāhā" at the end. || 19 ||
O Six-faced One, for one who is under the power of the weapon-mantra, there is neither the *bindu* nor even the *śikhā*;
likewise, those [mantras] with the *visarga* are known to be blazing and performers of terrible deeds.
The syllable consisting of the thirty-first [letter] joined with the seventh vowel,
and combined with the half of the letter *ka*, is proclaimed as the *kṣarikā* weapon-mantra.
These mantras are the subtle crests (śikhās), supreme and fulfilling all desires;
with all of these, one should always effect the transformation of oneself into Śiva.

Whenever one performs the ritual purification, at that very time one should perform the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the bodies of the wrathful deities for the sake of the mantra-siddhi of the noble practitioner.
Thus ends the chapter on the extraction of the Prāsāda mantra in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrī-Sarvajñānottara.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme rite of making [the self] Śiva;
by performing this correctly, a person truly becomes Śiva, and not otherwise.
First, one should purify the body by means of the five dhāraṇās;
having then become one whose body is purified, one should employ the mantras of Śiva. || 2 ||
Through the central channel (suṣumṇā), one should place the power that is both internal and external and whose form is space;
in its center, however, is the syllable *huṃ*, blazing with the brilliance of fire.
One should fix the mind upon that [point] where the prāṇa and apāna are joined;
liberation occurs through the upward thrust, accompanied by the syllable *huṃ*. (4)
In this way, effect the breaking of the knot; then one should begin the practice of *sādhana* again.
When [the breath] has been properly and completely restrained, the vital air (*vāyu*) flows upward. (5)
The one known as *yodghāta* is performed by one's own will when [the breath] is younger;
having withdrawn it by means of *pūraka*, the knower of mantras [should do so] with the heart.
One should place the living soul (jīva), consisting of the seed-syllable of peace (SĀNTA), upon the top of the syllable HŪM;
and within the crest of that HŪM, one should place the Puruṣa, whose form is composed of the seed-syllables.
Having meditated upon [the self] as solitary, subtle, become a drop (bindu), and free from affliction,
the yogi should then unite it with Śiva, the supreme cause.
In that which transcends Śiva, eternally peaceful and as pure as clear crystal,
by a single utterance alone, it is consecrated with one hundred thousand recitations.
Endowed with the state of oneness, one should enter the imperishable Śiva;
for the knower of reality, it is through the function of the seed-syllable, while in the case of others, it is through the function of the peak-syllable.
One should place the earthly seed-syllable with the heart-mantra, together with the watery one by means of the head-mantra.
One should employ within the mandalas the fire-mantra associated with the crest-lock (śikhā), the wind-mantra accompanied by the armor (kavaca), and the syllable *hoṃ* conjoined with the mantra. 12.
These [five] dhāraṇās, beginning with Aindrī, should be known by the best of teachers; and those kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are proclaimed as belonging to the Bindu. || 13 ||
Through the distinctions of *pradhāna* and *ādhāra*, these [energies] abide as one within the *praṇava*.
By means of knowledge, one should correctly understand these *kalās* as being gross, subtle, and mixed. (14)
Then, for the sake of purifying the body,
one should perform meditation upon a square, level, yellow [mandala], which is as firm and heavy as a diamond-limbed vajra.
Mounted upon the seat of the letter *la* and situated in the center of the heart-seed-syllable (*hṛdbīja*), one should purify it as it becomes wind, joined with five upward breaths (*udghāta*). (16)
One should meditate upon the orb of Varuṇa, which is semicircular, fluid, gentle, and possesses a luster equal to a pure kunda flower or the moon; it is adorned with a lotus in its center.

Situated in the center of the seat of the letter *va*, the head-seed [syllable] facing downwards should be purified as the element of fire by means of four upward breath-impulses (*udghāta*). || 18 ||
One should meditate upon that [deity] raining down, sounding, and being most cooling—the destroyer of the great force of the fire of poison and the noose of Time. 19.
One should meditate upon the mandala of Agni, which is well-proportioned, triangular, marked in its center by a śṛṅgāṭaka resembling a pomegranate flower.
One should purify the element of water by means of three upward thrusts (udghātas), [visualizing] the supreme seed-syllable called Śikhā mounted upon the seat of the letter Ra.
One should meditate upon the wind mandala, beginning from the feet, as it purifies one's own body, burning away impurities, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, appearing as a drop (*bindu*), and flickering.
The armor, which has the form of wind, is seated upon the seat of the letter Ya.
One should purify the earthly element joined with two upward breaths;
then one should contemplate the sky, which is all-pervading and accompanied by impurity.
Eternal, all-pervading, and tranquil, adorned with the power of the *bindu*,
the letter *ha* is entered by the syllable *oṃ* and does not abide within the *nāda*. (25)

One should purify that which has become empty by means of merely striking it with the *koṇa* [mudrā], and through various meditations combined with the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the maṇḍala. // 26 //
When the mind is properly stilled through breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), that is designated as concentration (dhāraṇā);
for by means of that very concentration, the entire universe is held, since it is composed of that [consciousness]. 27.
O Lord of Yogins, whatever the nature of that water of karma was which they entered,
you likewise became immortal with a perfectly purified body, knowing the proper rite.
Then, by means of etymological analysis, one should discern the path: "Which channel flows for me? In which does the person (pudgala) move? || 29 ||

In that regard, there is the destruction of the internal body and the interval between births; such is the state of his body when he has become disembodied and has entered into the eyes during his karmic activities.
One should perform [the practice] for that which is eternally risen and always present;
that which is in the left nostril is proclaimed as the *iḍā*. (31)
Piṅgalā is to be known as being on the right, while Suṣumnā is situated in the middle;
whichever channel has the greater flow of breath is the one that grants all desires.
When the *iḍā* channel is flowing, one should visualize the station of heaven;
the knower of yoga [visualizes] the *piṅgalā* channel as the lotus and the *suṣumnā* at the crown of the head.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in the heart; one should visualize Bhauma at the navel;
and one should meditate upon Śiva, the granter of boons who faces in all directions, at the end of the head.
One should worship the God at night and perform the fire-oblation (homa) during the day;
thereafter, meditation is prescribed for the twilights, while recitation (japa) is prescribed for both day and night. (35)

Recitation performed during the day is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), while that performed at night is of the nature of passion (rājasa). Recitation during the twilight (saṃdhyā) is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), accomplishing all goals.

The audible recitation is said to be tāmasa, while the whispered recitation is called rājasa; those who know the rules of recitation understand that the mental recitation performed with the mind is sāttvika.
A wise person should employ *tāmasa* recitation for those of cruel deeds, *rājasa* for subjugation and similar rites, and *sāttvika* for the attainment of divine powers. (38)
That recitation which is always performed through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāpatti) is declared to be *sāttvika*; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 39 ||
The wise man should always perform it in two ways: gross and subtle;
for by means of meditation, yogins indeed attain supreme perfection. (40)

The best of those who perform fire-offerings (homavittama) should meditate upon the gross mantra-form, complete with all its limbs, situated within the two paths in the sacrificial fire during worship.
But the seed of Śiva alone is devoid of all limbs;
it is not of the nature of birth, supremely pure, and is proclaimed to be subtle. || 42 ||

O Guha, the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is said to be night, whose nature is lunar; the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), pertaining to the sun, is declared to be the pure day. The equinox (viṣuva), however, is said to be the twilight (*sandhyā*) in the north... [43]

One should indicate the southern solstice for [the wind] blowing from the north; one should know the northern solstice for [the wind] blowing from the south; and at the midpoint, there is the equinox. (44)
When the wind flows equally through both nostrils, one should know that it is the equinox (viṣuva), a meritorious mantra consisting of both [the inhaled and exhaled breaths]. || 45 ||

O Peacock-bannered One, one should meditate on the equinox and the deities beginning with Candra and Mahendra as being situated in the southern solstice, contained within that which is called Iḍā, along the path of the ancestors.
One should meditate on Brahmā, Agni, Ravi, and Vāyu as they have resorted to the uttarāyaṇa; that which is situated within the Piṅgalā is called the Devayāna.
The wise man should meditate upon Ananteśa, Carudra, Sadāśiva, and Śiva as situated within the Suṣumnā during the equinox.
One should install the fourfold— knowledge of dharma, detachment, and sovereignty—
as well as the yoga-seat and the lotus, using the syllable *praṇava*.
The wise one should first place the *tattva* in the pericarp;
it pervades [the body] from below and above, and then one should again apply the *śakti*.

Then, by means of inhalation (pūraka), one should draw forth the life-force (jīva), which has become Śiva and is free from affliction— the supreme essence consisting of the seed-syllable of Śiva, situated within the crest-lock (śikhā).
One should place the extremely pure form of light in the middle of the topknot (śikhā), being equally drenched from above by nectar. 52.
Therefore, O Six-faced One, listen now to the true nature of the arrangement of mantras within this subtle body, according to their proper sequence.
Having placed the palms together for the rite of pacification (śānti), one should apply the Brahma-mantras, beginning with Īśāna, to the five fingers starting from the little finger. (54)
Then one should again employ the limbs, beginning with the heart;
thereafter, one should install the temple (prāsāda), which pervades the five [limbs] and faces in all directions.
Then one should perform the anointing, beginning from the feet up to the head.
One should place Īśāna five times on the head and [the other deities] on the four faces.
One should assign the fifth [mantra] among those spoken by the one of blazing splendor and the white-clad [Śiva] with the *praṇava*;
then, one should arrange the *aghora* [mantra] with the heart and other limbs, and the secret and left [limbs].
Beginning from the feet, one should assign Sadyojāta with all the limbs;
likewise, [one should assign it] to the heart, the neck, the two arms, the navel, and the abdomen.
The knower of mantras should place Bahurūpin on the back and the chest;
likewise in the secret place and the penis, as well as on the thighs and the knees.
One should place the left digits on the two calves, the buttocks, the hips, and the sides;
likewise on the two feet, the two hands, the nose, and the head. (60)
O knower of mantras, one should place the Sadyojāta-kalā on the external parts;
having placed the Netra-mantra on the eyes, one should again apply the ancillary limbs (aṅgas).
Having placed the heart-mantra on the heart, one should place the head-mantra on the head;
the crest-mantra on the crest, and the armor-mantra between the breasts.
When the weapon is in the region of the hand, one should then take recourse to meditation;
one should contemplate within oneself the very form that Śiva possesses.
Always perform this placement of the Śiva-mantras upon yourself;
having cast off the natural state, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva."
O Six-faced One, just as the arrangement is within the body, so it is also externally.
Just as I shall describe the external sacrifice, so too [is it performed] within the subtle body;
likewise indeed in the body of the disciple, and in the same way in the fire-offering (homa). || 65 ||
Thus ends the chapter on Paramīkaraṇa in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrī-Sarvajñānottara.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual for the external sacrifice (bāhyayāga),
which grants all desires, is secret, removes all sins, and is supreme.
Having adorned his own body with the mantras of Śiva in the proper sequence,
and having become one with Śiva with a thoroughly purified soul, he should begin the worship of Śiva.
Facing north and remaining pure, one should brandish the weapon;
by three claps of the hand, one should expel gross obstacles.
One should threaten them with the index finger and place the haṃsa-mantras;
then the practitioner of mantras should encircle that location again with the kavaca-mantra.
Then, one should indeed deploy the weapons in the cardinal and intermediate directions:
the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, and likewise the goad.
The mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus— these [are placed] in due order,
beginning from the eastern direction up to the domain of Īśāna.
Having placed the discus below, one should join the lotus above;
then, with perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should again worship the weapons.
Then, having withdrawn that subtle power which consists of nectar,
they indeed cause it— which is immeasurable and beyond the reach of the mind— to pervade both below and above. (8)
Then one should take up the *arghya* vessel and wash it with the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*;
afterwards, one should protect it both internally and externally with the *kavaca*.
Having taken recourse to the station of the Bindu, one should contemplate a lotus in the center; one should place the three principles (tattvas) therein and further apply the Śakti.
Having filled it with the five Brahmans, the limbs of Śiva,
and Śiva himself, that water, consecrated by mantras, is joined with fragrance and flowers.
O child, one should invoke the Supreme God, the Temple of supreme nectar,
who is embraced by his limbs and is as pure as clear crystal.
One should sprinkle with that [water] the substances prepared for the sake of the sacrifice;
O Śivā, nothing unsprinkled shall indeed become divine.
O Six-faced One, one should perform the worship with their own mantras according to the prescribed method for the deities, beginning with Dharma and ending with the Astra-mantra, excluding Śiva.

At the time of the fire-oblation (homa), the offering of the final oblation (saṃpūrṇāhuti), and the dedication of all ritual acts, it is prescribed that [the offerings] be made with the auspicious mantras of Śiva.
Knowledge of Dharma, detachment, and sovereignty— this quartet,
located in the southern direction, is established in the intermediate quarters with the syllable Om.
Having first visualized Śakti in the place of Brahmā,
one should then install the Yoga-pīṭha, followed by the stalk of Śakti and the lotus.
That [mandala] should have eight petals, with a pericarp occupying one-fourth of the space;
it is strewn with filaments occupying three parts and overspread with a network of rays. (18)
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalā, Balā, as well as Balapramathanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī. || 19 ||
Beginning from the leaf opposite [the practitioner] and extending as far as the leaf of Śaṅkara,
one should perform the placement upon the filaments and the petals with the Heart mantra.
One should place Manonmanī, the Śakti whose essence is the cause, in the center;
one should then conceive of Īśāna as the Śiva-void within the pericarp.
Furthermore, one should arrange the Mūrti-mantra to the northeast of Śiva;
having meditated upon the Pudgala as being white in color at the eastern face, [one should proceed].
One should place the one named Aghora in the south and Vāma in the north;
Sadyojāta, however, should be in the western part, and then the invocation (āvāhana) should take place.
Having invoked [the deity] with the Sadyojāta mantra, one should establish [him] with the Vāmadeva mantra;
with the Aghora mantra, one should effect his presence, and with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, one should offer the arghya.
Then one should make the entire manifest [deity] unmanifest in its characteristics;
endowed with the forms of the [respective] colors, one should again perform the worship.
One should place Īśāna fivefold upon the head and in the four faces;
the fifth [syllable] for those described as having blazing splendor and white [complexion] is indeed with the Praṇava.
One should apply the Aghora mantra to the heart and limbs, and the Guhya-vāma to the secret parts;
then, starting from the feet, one should perform the placement of Sadyojāta upon all the limbs.
The knower of mantras should place the Bahurūpaka mantra upon the heart, the neck, the two shoulders, the navel, the belly, the back, and the chest. (28)
One should place the left digits on the secret place, as well as the penis, the two thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, the two buttocks, the waist, and the sides. (29)
The feet, the hands, the nose, and the head are indeed the splendor of Lañjā;
thus, the Sadyojāta-kalā exists everywhere within all forms.
Having placed the Netra mantra upon the eyes, one should then apply the limbs;
having placed the Heart mantra upon the heart, one should place the Head mantra upon the head.
One should know the *śikhā* [mantra] for the crest-lock, the *kavaca* for the middle of the chest, and the *astra* for the region of the hands; then one should again apply the limbs (*aṅga*).
Having placed [the weapon] in the heart in the southeast (āgneyī), one should place the head in the northeast (īśānī);
one should assign the crest-lock (śikhā) in the southwest (nairṛtī) and place the armor (kavaca) in the northwest (vāyavī). || 33 ||
The knower of mantras, standing in the second enclosure, should place the Astra-mantra in all directions starting from the east, and the Gāyatrī in the intermediate directions.
In the third [circle], however, one should install the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), beginning from the east:
Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śiva, and again Uttama.
Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Amṛtadyuti,
Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍīśa— [these were] like the sun at the end of an eon.
All of them, assuming forms at will and bestowing the fruit of the body of sugarcane, are the lords of the Gaṇas;
they are located in the fourth direction, starting from the quarter of Kaubera (the North), in due order.
And likewise Diva, Caṇḍeśa, Mahākāla, Nandin,
Gaṇādhyakṣa, Bhṛṅgīśa, Vṛṣabha, and Skanda himself. (38)
The wise one should meditate on the presence [of the deity] as having a radiance equal to an undisturbed ruby;
furthermore, in the fifth enclosure, the world-protectors [should be meditated upon] in their respective order.
One should place [the deities] along the path of the weapon-mantra, possessing the luster of molten gold:
Indra, Pāvaka, Yama, and Nirṛti.
They know the syllable Om (Praṇava) to be the face of Water, Vāyu, Kubera, Īśāna, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, as well as Vidyeśvara and Gaṇeśa.
Having thus deposited the *bindu* of the world-protectors and the *visarga* within the sources of the weapons according to the prescribed rule, one should then worship Śiva.
Resembling pure crystal, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, his feet resting upon jewels, and marked with the conch, discus, and lotus; || 43 ||
His shanks, thighs, and feet were symmetrical; his joints were hidden, and his head was well-proportioned;
his hips and chest were broad, and his breast and shoulders were full.
With the tips of his fingers deeply red, long arms, and brilliant nails;
with thick arms, head, and shoulders, a deep navel, and a slender waist. (45)
He had a neck like a conch shell, well-proportioned limbs, and a radiant, full face;
his eyebrows, forehead, bimba-red lips, ears, and nose were perfect, as was the hair upon his head.
He is stainless, five-faced, and adorned with five heads above;
he has three eyes, ten arms, is peaceful, and is decorated with a crown of matted hair. (47)
The god bears the crescent moon, has eyes as broad as lotus petals,
sits in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), is serene, and has his eyes slightly closed. (48)
Seated upon the lion-throne of mantras, being fanned by excellent women,
his limbs anointed with divine perfumes, he was enchanting in his celestial garments.
Having thus meditated upon him who is complete with all the marks, adorned with all ornaments, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires, the practitioner of mantra [should proceed]. (50)
Then one should perform the rites such as bathing accompanied by mantras;
one should bathe [the deity] with the Sadyojāta seed-syllable and anoint [him] with the Kavaca mantra. (51)
With the Vāmadeva mantra, he should offer the garments and the girdle;
with the Īśāna mantra, however, he should offer the flowers, the crown, and the earrings.
The armlet, the sacred thread, the bracelet,
and the necklace should be offered with the Aghora mantra, while the incense should be offered with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
One should cause a lamp to be offered with the [mantra] of the eye, and again successively with the [mantras of the] enclosures (āvaraṇas).
Here, one should cause perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp to be presented. || 54 ||
Then one should offer the arghya, preceded by water for the feet and water for sipping;
having presented the arghya to the deity, one should then display the mudrās.
The salutation, the banner, the black-eared one, and the crest;
then the mudrās, the lotus, and the linga in the form of substance. (56)
These supreme accomplishments indeed bring about the presence of Śivī;
having smeared one's hands with fragrant substances, one should properly worship the mudrā. || 1 ||
One should first offer water for the feet (*pādya*) from the front to Śiva who has arrived with his two feet;
one should then place water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) in his mouths and the water for honor (*arghya*) upon his heads. (2)
One should offer the first *arghya* during the invocation, likewise at the end of the worship, and the third *arghya* for the deity during the dismissal. || 3 ||
Beginning from the eastern head, the knower of mantras should apply the fivefold arghya in the south, north, west, and in the center.
One should offer the *arghya* water again and again, both with the right hand and with the left;
it should be given to one facing upward, as well as to those facing toward oneself and those facing away.
One should offer the *arghya* facing the deity while he is established [in the ritual];
however, at the time of dismissal (*visarjana*), O son of Gaṅgā, the *arghya* should be offered with one's back turned away.
Such is the procedure for the arghya; now learn from me the substances [to be offered]:
various kinds of foods to be chewed, foods to be eaten, drinks, and so forth, as well as things to be licked and sucked.
Having offered everything with the heart-mantra as directed by the ritual manual, one should again present the food offering consecrated by mantras while reciting the [concluding] āvāhana mantras.
After that, once the fire has been well-kindled, he should perform the ritual task;
having performed the offering to the spirits according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, he should present the bali-offering.

The practitioner of mantra should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits, consisting of all kinds of cooked food mixed together, accompanied by water and rice-grains, and provided with flowers and incense.
Then, having washed his hands and feet and sipped water (ācānta), he should sip water again;
thereafter, having entered the sanctuary, the wise man should perform his recitation (japa). || 11 ||

Having prostrated and propitiated the Lord, the knower of mantras, relying upon meditation and through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), should always recite [the mantra] with a one-pointed mind fixed on the crest-lock (śikhā).
Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), observing silence, with a rosary held in his hand,
having assumed the svastika posture, he remains with his body and head held straight. (13)
The yogin and mantra-practitioner whose mind is focused on nothing else, having attained identity with that [reality] and relying upon both non-duality and duality, attains perfection before long.
Thus ends the section on worship in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrī Sarvamantrānottara.
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual procedure for the fire-offering (agnikārya),
which is the foundation of all accomplishments and bestows fruits both in this world and the next.
First, the wise one should sprinkle the sacrificial pit with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra;
thereafter, he should encircle it in due order with the Kavaca-mantra.
O Six-faced One, one who knows the ritual procedure should perform the scraping again with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra),
and afterwards, the sprinkling with water using the armor-mantra (kavaca).
One should then place the seat (viṣṭara) within the center of the pit with the syllable Om;
thereafter, one should place upon it the Śakti, which resembles a thousand flashes of lightning.
The large-eyed woman in her season [is attained] by constant practice with the *yonimudrā*;
the seed-syllable of fire (*ra*), ignited from above, is conjoined with the four vowels and the nasal sound (*anusvāra*) above.
The Haṃsa multiplied by sixteen is declared to be this Śakti;
having honored it with perfumes and flowers and having offered the Arghya according to the rule, the knower of the ritual [proceeds].

Then, for the purpose of fully satisfying Śiva, one should prepare the fire; [the syllable] is formed by omitting the fourth [letter] and joining it with the sixth from the bottom [of the alphabet]. (7)
That very fire, known as Haṃsa, is the accomplisher of all goals;
having kindled the sacrificial fire in either a copper vessel or a clay bowl, [one should proceed]. (p. 42) 8.
One should sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra and again apply the seed-syllable;
thereafter, the knower of the ritual procedure should encircle it with the Kavaca-mantra.
Having worshipped [the deity] three times in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should deposit it through the path of the womb (yonimārga);
then, one should again recite the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) with the Sadyojāta mantra.
O Six-faced One, the bathing in the Gaṅgā occurs in this manner within the sacrificial fire;
having worshipped Vāmadeva with one's head bowed, one should then recite his mantra.
The *puṃsavana* rite has been performed; now hear likewise concerning the *sīmantonnayana*.
One should worship the deity with the *aghora* mantra and then recite the *śikhā-bīja*.
The demarcation of the fire's boundary is performed according to the Śaiva rite;
having worshipped it with the Kavaca mantra, one should recite the Tatpuruṣa mantra for the pervasive Lord.
Having thus performed the birth-rite (jātakarma), one should then designate the name;
having worshipped with the Īśāna mantra, one should also transform the weapon-mantra (astra).
Then he should cause her to hear his name: "You are Śivāgni, the consumer of oblations.
At her birth, there is the lotus-mudrā; at the joining of the fire, the liṅga-mudrā.
In all rites, the seed-syllables *ni* and *ru* are declared to be harsh regarding cessation (*nirodha*).
Having thus properly consecrated the fire, one should [apply] the mudrās with the mantras in their proper sequence. (16)
Then one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the ritual procedure seen in the scriptures;
one should spread darbha grass with the heart-seed syllable and cause the enclosing sticks (paridhi) to be placed.
Furthermore, one should worship the gods with their tips pointing eastward and northward:
Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, together with Ananteśa. (p. 43) 18.

Beginning from the east, one should place the seats for the Viṣṭaras in that order according to the Gāyatrī; then, taking recourse to the south-eastern direction, one should set down the vessel of clarified butter.
Having first performed the act of placing [the vessel] on the fire, he should afterwards perform the rinsing and other rites;
then, having cut with his fingernail darbha grass-blades measuring one span in length.
Holding [the vessel] with the thumb and ring finger, perform the sprinkling of ghee;
then the mantra-practitioner performs the immersion, facing the ghee like a blue lotus.
Having heated the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles in the fire and wiped them all around, one should touch the entire surface— the tip, the middle, and the base— with the ring finger.

One who knows the ritual procedure should place the sacrificial offerings, such as clarified butter and the like, on the southern side, and likewise on the northern side; with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, he should perform all the rites.
Then, O Six-faced One, one should pour [the liquid] from the mouth with the Brahma-mantras in due order; thereafter, one should perform the reopening with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra).
Having performed the expiation with the Śiva-weapon (śivāstra), one should offer clarified butter;
likewise, one should perform the threefold offering for Śiva, Soma, and Vighneśvara.
Then, having gratified the fire and offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in due order,
one should then perform the placement of the seat (āsana-vinyāsa) as prescribed.
Having properly worshipped Śiva with perfumes and flowers in due order according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should then commence the fire sacrifice (homa).
When the fire has been purified with abundant fuel, well-kindled,
crackling amidst the coral-like embers, he for whom the oblation is offered attains success. (28)
Arciṣmān, Paṇḍita, Śikha, Sugandhin, Laghuvikrama, Sniṃdha, Pradakṣiṇāvarta, and Jātavedas are the perfected ones. || 29 ||
One who bears the mark of Viṣṇu should draw on the ground; [if it is] white, black, or faded, and if it is foul-smelling and rough, no success is found there.
One should offer oblations right there until the fire becomes purified;
when the fire is purified, purification [of the disciple] occurs, otherwise it would be fruitless. (31)
Therefore, having understood this, one who is purified should always perform the oblation with the specific enumeration of offerings for all mantras, beginning with Śiva. (32)
Having increased the fire-oblation tenfold, one should perform it for Śiva by the measure of one hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even a hundred thousand.
The power of Brahmā is said to be one part less than that of the limbs of Śiva, the Vidyeśvaras, the Gaṇeśvaras, and the foremost among the world-protectors and their weapons. (34)
One should perform the offering of the final oblation accompanied by dhāraṇā,
while mentally recollecting, O dear one, the supreme nectar flowing forth.
The mantra-practitioner should utter the word "pūrṇā" as the mantra equivalent to the full oblation;
he should then recollect this [mantra] ending with "vauṣaṭ," preceded by "idam astu amṛtam. (36)
Having offered one's mind to the mantra and having adorned one's body with the mantra,
one should perform the fire-oblation with a single-pointed mind, having attained identity with the mantra.
By means of that supreme reality of sound, he shall become a partaker of the fruit of accomplishment. || 38 ||
Having bowed with devotion to the Lord of Gods and having praised Him, one should ask for forgiveness at the conclusion;
then, having withdrawn [the visualization], the practitioner of mantra should offer the recitation to the subjects.
Whatever has been done and whatever you shall do—all that is your own good deed;
for you, O Śiva, the knower of all, are my refuge and no other protector indeed exists for me.
Then, having worshipped the deity again according to the prescribed rite, one should dismiss the deity;
thereafter, with a concentrated mind, one should dismiss the fire once the ritual action has been completed.
One should know that the offering of perfumes and flowers made to a deity who has been dismissed is *nirmālya*; likewise, the garments and ornaments [offered] are to be avoided.
Having worshipped the Kūṭa, one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa;
one must avoid consuming the *nirmālya*, giving it away, or stepping over it. || 43 ||
Having sipped water and performed the ritual sprinkling (uddhūlana), one whose self is purified should begin the meal;
then, having washed the vessel according to the prescribed rule, one should eat.
Having performed the wrapping in that very same manner, the one who knows the ritual procedure should then place [the object] within it with the Śiva-mantra, the Śivagāyatrī, and the Hṛdaya-mantra.
