One should offer five oblations with the heart-mantra and dedicate the remainder to Śiva.
Having sipped water and become pure, one should meditate upon Śiva and recite [the mantra] again. (46)
Having released the vessel at the end of the recitation, speak what is true and beneficial;
for the sake of some worldly transaction, one may eat, but then one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again.
O Six-faced One, the fire-ritual, recitation, sacrifice, yoga,
and initiations [should be performed] in a secret, delightful place on a well-purified patch of ground. (48)
Thus ends the section on fire-rituals in the Kriyāpāda of the Sarvajñānottara.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the purification of the earth’s surface, as well as its examination and formal acquisition. 1.
Endowed with fragrance and a pleasant taste, white, red, or tawny in color,
even if mixed with dust, this auspicious Bhrami-blossom accomplishes all goals.
One should examine a plot of ground that slopes toward the northeast, is smooth, black, or of auspicious appearance, situated near a body of water, and pure.
Whatever color and whatever fragrance is beautiful, that indeed is found there;
[the ground] should be devoid of hair, bones, and thorns, and free from pits and saline soil. (4)
On ground free from all defects, having struck it three times with the hand, one should prepare the sacrificial bed.
One should moisten it with fragrant water and the auspicious water of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
then, having bathed and being purified, one should again wash it with clean garments.
Then, with water filtered through a cloth in a jar made from *akālamūla* roots,
and with *kuṭaja*, *vaṣa*, *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, and *mudgara* [wood], [he should perform the ritual].
Having made the ground level like the surface of a mirror, one should take possession of it;
it may be made of baked bricks or likewise of pure wood.
Alternatively, having constructed a pure sacrificial pavilion made of clay,
one should make it twice as long as its width and one part in breadth.
On the third part, at the door, measuring one and a half cubits,
one should arrange two parts for the mandala and one part for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should perform cruel rites in the intermediate directions and auspicious rites in the cardinal directions;
one should construct a very solid, square sacrificial pavilion.
One should then construct a square enclosure, variegated and richly adorned with paintings, and likewise a circular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should fashion the yoni situated at the center above the girdle;
then, the most learned in the scriptures should make the girdle even.
It should be four fingers in height, firm, marked with the lotus of consciousness,
and one cubit in measure, both in the middle and at the top.
One should fashion it with three ridges, perfectly even and beautiful to behold;
the needle and the bud-like tip should be made like the trunk of an elephant.
One should fashion a beautiful bow-receptacle from the center of the upper part of the girdle;
above that, it should again be made firm with wood, either projecting upwards or level.
One should construct it with a canopy, adorned with garlands and provided with lattices;
one should know that to be beautiful and the bestower of the fruits of all desires. || 17 ||
Having made the ground perfectly pure and having taken possession of it, one should perform the sacrifice again;
[using] a full *vardhanī* vessel consecrated with the *aghora-astra* mantra. (18)
Having performed this, what would the wise ones place? They would place a circumambulation (pradakṣiṇā) that is exceedingly high;
along its path, the jar was slowly raised by the preceptor.

Having caused [the practitioner] to frown with all his might, one should cause him to place [the vessel]; that indeed is the supreme pacification of the flood of obstacles within the northeastern mandala. (20)
Placed upon a lotus in front, resting on the seven grains,
it is washed with the weapon-mantra (astra-bīja) and bound around the neck with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Placed upon a female figure, it is fumigated with sandalwood and agallochum incense,
filled with water purified by a cloth, and endowed with the five jewels.
Provided with all medicinal herbs and adorned with all fragrances, it should have its neck bound with gold, or else with a cord around the neck. (23)
O Guha, Śiva is thus beautiful and delightful, joined with mango sprouts, covered with white cloth, and presided over by Śivā.
Having worshipped at the beginning of the sacrifice, one should perform the ritual bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice;
likewise, when taking possession [of a site], there should be a Vāstu-sacrifice, and a further sacrifice for the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Having prepared the Śivāsana for Śiva, the Supreme Self,
one should collect the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) and the offerings of food (naivedya).
Then he should consecrate those [implements], and subsequently, in due order, the disciples;
for them, he should provide the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), sacrificial porridge (caru), and a tooth-stick, all consecrated with mantras.
One should offer the *kṣarikā* seven times with the heart-mantra;
then, by that destruction of the ritual procedure, no accomplishment (*siddhi*) exists. || 28 ||
O Six-faced One, one should know that the tooth-stick is auspicious when it is otherwise than this; that is, when its tip points toward the directions beginning with the northeast. (29)
The supreme practitioner shall accomplish all rites through the *dhātu*. One should recognize that as auspicious, for it bestows the fruits of all desires. (30)
Thus ends the chapter on the acquisition of the ground in the Kriyāpāda of the Sarvajñānottara.
Henceforth, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall indeed proclaim the ritual procedure for the five products of the cow; listen to it in its true essence, O Six-faced One.
I shall now describe, in due order, the preparation of the sacrificial porridge (caru) and the vessel for it:
cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with kuśa grass.
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are declared to be the destroyer of great sins.
One should worship with clarified butter using the Īśāna mantra, but with milk using the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
Curd is prescribed with the Aghora mantra, cow dung with the Sadyojāta,
cow urine with the Vāmadeva, and kuśa-water with the Gāyatrī.
Having stirred everything contained in the copper vessel with the heart-mantra, one should mentally divide it into three portions: for the Deity, for oneself, and likewise [for the guest].
Having drawn it out like a son for his disciple, he himself should drink what has been consecrated by Śiva;
then, having washed the vessel as before and wrapped it in the same manner, he should set it down.
O Six-faced One, having again placed the five Brahmans upon the throat with the armor-mantra (*varma*) recited over a thread, one should fill it once more with milk.
One should cook it with the fire of Śiva and slowly fashion it with the armor-mantra (varman),
using rice, śyāmāka, nīvāra, or even śāli and vrīhi.
Having washed the rice grains, one should subsequently cast them [into the vessel] and stir them with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
likewise, one should employ the *hṛdaya*, the *śiras*, the *śikhā*, and the *gāyatra*.
Performing the recitation (*japa*), the mantra-practitioner should accomplish the *caru* mixed with ghee; he should prepare it in such a way that the food becomes as desired. (10)
Having brought it down, one should recite the pure mantra as long as one desires nirvāṇa;
thereafter, one should divide it into three parts, just as previously described.
Having performed the ritual action, one should consume that which belongs to oneself and is associated with the disciple;
without touching it with the teeth, one should take the measure established for the five fingers.

Mounted upon a reed of darbha grass along with his disciples, having conquered his senses, devoted to meditation on the countryside, observing silence, he was well-protected by the weapon of the rampart.
Having seen the binding nooses and bones at the end of their dreams, all the disciples, having become pure and composed, relate them to the Guru. (14)
Through auspicious [means] one attains the desired accomplishment, while through inauspicious ones one encounters suffering;
therefore, seeing that it bestows suffering, one who has attained accomplishment should not employ it. 15.
Upon seeing a bad dream, the practitioner of mantras, having performed one thousand recitations of the *hem* syllable,
should perform an initiation that pertains to this world but is devoid of supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
Whether it be a bright river, a stream, the ocean, or even a morass—
that great and difficult obstacle which one crosses over, he attains success.
For them, there may occur, in reverse order, the fear of disease or death, imprisonment, the destruction of their livelihood, or even travel to a foreign land. (18)
He who, while lying down, sees in a dream the destruction of his cattle, horses, or elephants, or [the loss] of his garments, ornaments, and elephants, for him no success is found. (19)
But by obtaining these [mantras] beforehand, one shall attain desired objects;
he who, having seen them, does not sleep until the sun has risen. (20)
If one dreams of the bright fortnight, a funeral pyre, or even being strewn with thorns, yet has one's head struck off at the end of the dream, for such a person no success is found.

Yāmya, Hālāhala, Krodhana, Bandhavāmukha, and then the Sūlaganas, as well as the other six directions. (131)
Likewise, others such as the Hulahulas abide within the domain of Time (Kāla).
Above that, however, there is another, the principle of Māyā (Māyātattva), which is extremely difficult to cross.
Having a fissure like the interior of a *maṇḍavaka* fruit and possessing a luster like yellow orpiment,
the goddess Māyā, who assumes many forms, resides in its center.
Just as the entire world, both mobile and immobile, was deluded,
so too was it enveloped by a mass of rays resembling sapphire in hue.
It is surrounded by thousands and tens of millions of moving drops;
there are three who move to the left, and therein [is] the fair-eyed one who moves to the left.
O Six-faced One, those who perform non-left (i.e., right) actions are born as left-handed ones;
they cause the graceful movement of the limbs and are colored by affection for the limbs. 136.
(70) O Skanda, men who cast deceptive snares with hypocrisy, who captivate with hypocritical speech, and who are born from the white illusion (māyā-śukla-sambhava), are to be known as such. 137.
They are prone to much idle chatter, devoted to falsehood and deceitful conduct;
or else, they are like those who have emerged from all the essential principles of the Samudāvika school. (138)
Understand from me as it is being proclaimed this "three-fold impurity," which is pervasive and swift;
for whatever reality possesses a reality that is superior at birth. (139)
O Guha, that [individual soul] would also possess that same nature even at the time of dissolution;
for thus, the essential nature of all principles is established as being of the nature of consciousness.
Understand from me those Rudras who have been mentioned there in brief:
Gaganīśa, Asādhya, and likewise both Hari and Hara. (141)
Daśona, Mahāvīrya, Trigala, and likewise Gopati—
these six-faced ones are situated as the encasements (saṃpuṭa) of the principle of Māyā.
Now listen as I describe those who are situated even above that:
Kṣamuśa, Brahmā, Hantā, and another, Vidyeśāna. (143)
Vidyeśa and Śiva, with Ananta as the sixth, are proclaimed;
all of them are remembered as being free from pride and devoid of delusion and attachment. (144)
They are the liberators from the bonds of illusion and the breakers of the snare-like net;
then, O Six-faced One, above that there exists another, the principle of Vidyā (Vidyātattva). 145.
Slightly yellow and very pure, resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree;
there, the lords of the vidyās are to be known as having a luster equal to that of rubies. (146)
Blazing, stainless, subtle, all-pervading, and facing every direction—
from that [source] have issued forth the mantras, which possess the characteristics of the five limbs. (147)
The Vidyās should be known in the same way, as well as the Mantras of the Vidyās that are mixed;
all of them are inconceivable, possessors of arrows, and all have bliss as their stride. || 148 ||
All are all-pervading; all are accomplishers of every purpose.
All consist of the four kinds of nectar: earth, water, fire, and air. 149.
All possess identical qualities, yet the differences among listeners result in distinct fruits;
however, due to the inconceivable differences in the hands [of the teachers], there are further distinctions among the supreme Śivas through the various mantras.
He remains established for the sake of bestowing grace, acting as a witness to all actions;
[he knows] the location, the action, the disposition, the deity, and indeed the pervasion.
The Soul of the Universe proceeds by observing the divisions of the fields of action;
for such, O Six-faced One, is the distinction of mantras for one who has transcended the status of a minister.
Now, listen to me as I describe both non-duality and duality:
however many beings there may be, they all abide within the totality of principles (tattvas). || 153 ||
O Six-faced One, as many as are the forms, names, and lineages of those [deities], so many are recorded as the divisions of this bodiless body. (154)
Such is the nature of Śiva’s Vidya, which resides within their bodies;
it exists like a shadow-form, subtler than the gross and subtler still than the subtle.
In the partless [state], O Guha, there is a form that is utterly beyond parts; it is a form free from breath, dharma, and so forth, and devoid of the fruits of pleasure and pain.
He bestows [the fruit] in the form of various means (upāya), in accordance with each respective quality (dharma).
Thus, in this investigation of knowledge (vidyā), there is indeed a division of the mantras of Śiva. (157)
The wise know that the distinctions of the bodies and likewise the distinctions of the principles (tattvas) are well-known;
above Vidyā, however, there is another [level], namely the enclosure of the Vidyēśas.
O Skanda, it has the luster of a blazing fire, is slightly red, and perfectly pure;
the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) abide within it by virtue of their pervasive power.
Viṣṇu, resembling the fire of a *liṅga* and blazing with rays like lightning,
stood there in the center, O Mahāsena, surrounded like a wheel.
Endowed with the wheel of power (śakticakra), they should exercise their authority in due order;
O Six-faced One, [they shall possess] the mantras and tantras along with their secrets and ritual procedures (kalpa).
The high-souled ones of immeasurable splendor, belonging to the Rudras, declare that their palaces, seats, couches, ramparts, ornaments, and weapons [are all made of gold]. (162)
May all [beings] abide as composed of mantra, fulfilling every desire according to their wish;
may there be mastery over the sciences (vidyā) and sovereignty through the bestowal of the bliss of divine nectar. 163.
With soft forehead-bands that emit hair with curled tips, with eyebrows shaped like the bow Pināka, and with elevated chests; || 164 ||
With ears like mountains of light, with auspicious eyes like lotuses, and with the full expanse of their faces resembling the orb of the moon. || 165 ||
With lips that were slightly coppery, elevated, and full; with the tips of their noses graced by being prominent; and with rows of teeth that were not too high, even, glossy, and pure. || 166 ||
With ears resembling rubies, dark blue, and not causing distress; with well-concealed roots, symmetrical, hairless, glossy, and soft. (167)
With ears like conch-shells and partings of hair [marked by them], with arms as graceful as lotus stalks, with rounded, firm, and full breasts that are plump and elevated; || 168 ||
Their waists were slender with deep, rounded navels;
they possessed the splendor of waves upon the three folds of skin, which caused the mass of their body hair to tremble.
With beautiful interiors bristling with horripilation, with hidden bone-joints, and with charming private regions resembling the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree; || 170 ||
With thighs auspiciously marked, soft as the touch of the core of a plantain tree,
with hidden knees and ankles, and with broad, radiant hips.
With well-proportioned shanks and even feet, endowed with auspicious marks, his palms and the tips of his feet were deep red and marked with the conch, the discus, and the lotus. || 172 ||
With fingers that were very white, well-proportioned, and possessed of thin, high, and radiant nails;
with smooth skin, beautiful lines, and endowed with all auspicious marks. || 173 ||

But the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) are always served by those whose limbs are anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine ornaments, even though they are constantly oppressed by hunger. 174.
Accompanied by his own troops wearing celestial garments, adorned with divine garlands and unguents,
and by Rudras of various forms whose splendor was equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
Above that, there is another auspicious realm consisting of all sovereign powers, created by those endowed with the power of divine knowledge who are the agents of creation and destruction. (176)
Sadāśiva is the supreme reality, as pure and stainless as clear crystal;
upon that supremely pure seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) resides the Vidyā of the Great-Souled One.
(Aligned with the principles of Dharma and so forth,) it is joined by feet [at its base], adorned with a lotus in the center,
extending to beautiful filaments, and spreading out with a thousand petals. (178)
It is joined on the outside with eight lotuses of pure nature, distinguished by pure powers, and adorned with the limbs of Brahmā. || 179 ||
It is surrounded by the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) stationed at the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and by perfected yogis;
there dwells the Blessed Lord Hara, the sovereign of all principles (tattvas).
Sadāśiva is all-pervasive, omnipresent, the embodiment of mantra, beyond the material world, and supreme;
he is endowed with infinite splendor and possesses an immeasurable succession of qualities. || 181 ||
Possessing infinite power and enjoyment, seated upon an infinite throne,
the Supreme Lord divided his own body into eight parts.
With a tranquil mind, one should remain [focused] from Ananta up to Śikhaṇḍin;
above that is the pure, all-pervading principle of Bindu (baindava-tattva).
That supreme, infinite light-form of the principles (tattvas) exists there;
O Skanda, the Bindu is situated therein, as pure as clear crystal.

Having the form of a *kadamba* flower cluster and garlanded with shimmering rays, he is indeed both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), as well as both with and without parts (*sakalaniṣkala*). (185)

Śiva should be known as fivefold: as the subtle (sūkṣma) and as the one whose parts are divided (bhinnakala). That which is joined with the parts (kalā), beginning with Śānti, is recited as Sakala. || 186 ||
Partless, absolute, all-pervasive, and both with and without parts—united with Jvālinī and the others, this is proclaimed as the subtle. || 187 ||
O Six-faced One, the Bindu is said to have its nature divided by the sixteen vowels;
from that, O Six-faced One, its division is infinite in all the scriptures. (187)
In mantras and in the Mātṛkā, there is nowhere anything without the Bindu;
she is the partless Supreme Power (Parāśakti), inconceivable and facing in all directions. 188.
Extremely subtle, stainless, eternal, infinite, and bestowing liberation, she indeed unfolds within the principles and within all principles whatsoever. (189)
Thus, this entire world is of a single form within the Single Vehicle;
above this, it is without support, without foundation, and free from affliction.
It is immovable, all-pervasive, peaceful, and devoid of creation and destruction;
indeed, it arises from the conjunction of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, as well as from knowledge and passion. 191.
From the conjunction of Kalā and Kāla, from the union with Ananta, the principle of Māyā;
likewise, Vidyā and Sadāśiva arise from the union of Bindu and Śakti. || 192 ||
O Skanda, creation arises in sequence from the power of the drop (bindu) and so forth,
beginning with the earth and extending up to the principle of the drop (vaidavatatva).
One should understand reality from reality as it is established in direct perception;
O Six-faced One, beginning with the earth-tattva, one should likewise [understand] the deities. (194)
Just as sovereignty is mutually concealed [by the levels], so too is power concealed;
whatever names belong to the principles (tattvas), those same names apply to the lords of those principles as well. (195)
Having understood this, the mantra-practitioner should apply [the practice] toward that which he desires to attain;
for those who abide within all the principles (tattvas) above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), [he should act accordingly]. || 196 ||
Completely liberated from old age and death, and free from the afflictions of dualities—for them, whatever body there may be, no fear exists anywhere. (197)
O Guha, [the Lord] creates, destroys, and maintains the entire universe;
during the period of maintenance, He enjoys that sovereignty which has been described. (198)
At the time of dissolution, having become devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), they enter together with the principles (tattvas);
at the time of creation, they are born again in succession along with their respective principles.

Furthermore, one who knows the true nature of things understands that the rising, setting, and abiding of these occur in this way: whatever is eternally dependent upon something else, in reality belongs to that very thing.
At that time, he too becomes devoted to that [state],
just as the internal intervals have been described in terms of their pervasions by powers.
Likewise, O Skanda, the intermediate states should be understood in relation to rising, setting, and so forth; for one who knows Śiva, there is no rising or setting. 202.
For, since all principles ultimately abide within consciousness, the self, which is bound by these very principles, is conjoined with all phenomena. (203)
No one else is able to bestow these initiations, which are of the nature of Śiva and must be avoided [by others]. || 204 ||
Thus ends the chapter on the Paths (*adhvaprakaraṇa*) in the *Kriyāpāda* of the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*.
Henceforth, I shall explain [the nature] of the unawakened embodied being,
who is bound by all principles (tattvas) and consists of all phenomena (dharmas).
Listen now to the supreme and auspicious initiation, which bestows union with Śiva, for one engaged in the practice of animal sacrifice who seeks to wipe away beginningless impurity.
For whichever deity there may be a seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of one syllable,
it is joined with the fire-seed (*vahni-bīja*), conjoined with the letters *a* and *ā*.
(77) Then, the sixth [syllable] joined with the seed-syllable of wind (vāyu),
conjoined with a *bindu* on its head, is proclaimed by the mantra-master for all [purposes]. || 4 ||
That single syllable is further divided by twelve morae (mātrās);
it is declared that the short vowels constitute the Brahman, while one should indicate the limbs (aṅgas) by means of the long vowels.
The three principles (tritatva) joined with the bindu are proclaimed as the three eyes;
they are remembered as being with the visarga when they are the weapons (astra), and devoid of both bindu and nāda.
Having worshipped the gods in due order according to the procedure taught by Śiva,
and having performed libations as extensively as possible, one should then commence the initiation.
Having fasted, being pure, having bathed, sipped water, and wearing washed garments—
with their feet washed and sprinkled— he should cause the ṛṣis to enter after addressing them with mantras.
Having touched [the disciple] with the five Brahmans, the limbs of Śiva, and the Praṇava,
one should place the Eye-mantra upon the eyes and then perform the binding of the eyes.
With a garment made of dukūla silk, or of flax (vedāṅga), or likewise of cotton— new,
with a hundred threads, white, and smooth.
Accompanied by a handful of flowers, one should invoke Dakṣiṇāmūrti with a mind purified by the Guru, holding darbha grass in hand and well-consecrated by mantras.
The disciple should touch the right knee of the preceptor with the tip of a *darbha* blade;
then, having taken hold [of the cord] and withdrawn the bonds, he should perform the fire-oblation (*homayet*).
The knower of the ritual procedure likewise [employs] the Heart-mantra and the two Weapon-mantras;
then, in sequence, the letter *ya*, which transcends the classes [of consonants], and the Prāsāda-mantra.
Having first consecrated them with the seed-syllables, one should employ them in relation to dharma and adharma.
Regarding dharma, the tongue is to be praised; adharma is said to be the left [tongue]. (15)
Raudrī is established in both; situated there, one should perform the oblation for both.
The phonemes differentiated by the three principles (tattvas) are here called the triad of powers (śaktitraya).
But in the Dharma that transcends all attributes (varṇātīta), the dharmas are indeed the Middle Way;
furthermore, one should offer both dharma and adharma, mixed together, with serene clarity.
Alternatively, O Skanda, the wise one should offer both of those— dharma and adharma mixed together— as an oblation by means of the Śivatatva in its sakala form.
The Lord is conjoined with the letters *a* and *au*, situated at the end of the *haṃsavarga*, accompanied by the letter *m*, and impelled by fire and wind. (19)
When the sixth [vowel] is joined with the bindu upon the head (m),
it is designated as the Śiva-tattva, which pervades all beings in their entirety.
In whichever reality (tattva) a particular Lord resides, one should conceive of Śiva as being there;
one should perform all the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) in that reality by means of His mantras.
By means of all the duties toward a husband, cast aside the ways of a beast;
delight in those very duties toward a husband, for they are indeed the true dharma.
One should again offer oblations in sequence for the station, birth, lordship, the attainment of its enjoyment, authority, and dissolution. (23)
The knower of the ritual procedure should first join the *tattva* in the center of the sacrificial pit;
the mantra for all the *tattvas* is one's own name during the rite of grasping. (24)

O knower of reality, having seized the bound soul (paśu) within that [reality], one should place him into the womb of the Gāyatrī, which has been prepared according to the ritual procedure of one's own mantra. (25)
In the rite of seizing a sacrificial animal, one should visualize the tip of the nose as the fixed point,
and [the deity] in the form of a mass of radiant energy (*tejapiṇḍa*).

Having struck [the seed] with the weapon-mantra (astra-bīja) and the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should perform the rite of conception (garbhādāna) with the Sadyojāta-mantra; this is traditionally taught as the rite for the birth of a son (vāsu-puṃsavana).

One should employ the mantra beginning with "sumanasaḥ" for the birth-rite (jātakarman) of the person; the mantra beginning with "īśānaḥ" for the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa), and the "hṛdaya" mantra for the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana).
One should offer oblations with the *śiras* mantra for authority (*adhikāra*), with the *śikhā* mantra for enjoyment (*bhoga*),
with the seed-syllable of the eye (*netrabīja*) for sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and with the *kavaca* mantra for dissolution (*laya*).
With ten oblations for each [limb], and with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) by Śiva,
one should perform the purification of the ten channels (srotas) in successive order using the Brahma-aṅgas.
With Śiva, one should perform the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi) among all the principles;
likewise, one should offer oblations for the severing of bonds (pāśaccheda), their burning, and for expiation (prāyaścitta).
Having focused the reality within the principles of reality, one should obstruct the hells with the utterance of *huṃ phaṭ*.
Having first separated [the soul] from Jyeṣṭhā and then from Raudrī as well, one should extract it;
O Ṣaṇmukha, this rite must be performed according to this procedure for each and every tattva.
One should undertake this in great detail on the terrestrial plane (bhūrloka), which is the field of action;
however, within the principle (tattva) of Kālāgnirudra, one should purify the state of Kālāgni.
Having experienced the conditions of hellish beings in hell, one should lead them to the state of a *kūśmāṇḍa*.
But by performing this placement (*nyāsa*) in the seventh subterranean realm (*pātāla*), one should liberate them. (35)
Then, above that, he produced the principle of Hāṭaka in the world of beings (Bhūrloka);
by means of Sadyojāta, he produced the state of stationary things, and by means of his own self, the state of moving creatures.

One should perform the oblation in successive order: the state of being a bird with the *ghorarūpa* mantra, the state of being a deer with the *puruṣa* mantra, and the state of being a beast with the *īśabīja* mantra.
Having offered eleven oblations with the mantras, the knower of the ritual procedure should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and Aghora mantras.
One should cause the embodied soul to offer oblations for its state as a Śūdra, and then successively for the Vaiśya and the others;
likewise, one should perform the rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).

The ceremony of going out [from the house], as well as the first feeding of solid food, the rite of going out with the *hṛdinī* [verse], and the tonsure ceremony are indeed prescribed by the knowers of the Veda. (40)
Then the initiation (upanayana) should be performed in sequence with the ten limbs of Brahman:
the girdle, the sacred thread, the staff, the black antelope skin, and austerity.
Vedic study, the tending of the sacred fires, the twilight worship, begging for alms, respectful salutation, silence, celibacy, tranquility, and self-restraint. || 42 ||

Attendance upon the guru, recitation of mantras, freedom from blame, gentleness and straightforwardness, non-violence, truthfulness, lack of malice, renunciation, forbearance, and absence of backbiting. (43)
Compassion toward living beings, freedom from greed, absence of intoxication, modesty that is not fickle, splendor tempered by patience, purity that is stainless, and non-injury— these are constant.
One should offer all these, in their proper sequence, ten times within the *gāyatrī* [mantra]:
the *trāyuṣa*, the *upākarma*, the *godāna*, and the *mahāvrata*. (45)
One should offer the Naiṣṭhika and the Asidhāra oblations with the Pāśupata mantra;
thereafter, those [oblations] are declared to be for the purification of the limbs of Śiva.
One should again perform the union with the wife using the limbs of Brahmā;
having fashioned a wife out of darbha grass, one should unite her with the syllable "Om. (47)
With each of the ten mantras, the practitioner should offer ten oblations;
these constitute the Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Vājapeya, Ukthya, and Ṣoḍaśī sacrifices.
The Atirātra and the Aptoryāma are recorded as the Soma-saṃsthās;
[these are performed] with the limbs of Brahmā, the Śiva-gāyatrī, the Mahāstra, and Śiva himself.
One should offer twenty oblations for the purification of each [deity],
and thereafter, in all rites of consecration, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should employ Śiva, who has leaped forth and showers nectar;
he performs the fire-oblation with Śiva in whatever purificatory rite.
Except for the single *pūrṇāhuti*, one should perform that [rite] twice;
however, at the conclusion of the *somasaṃsthā* sacrifices, one should offer it once with each of all the mantras.
One should offer an oblation of curd, milk, ghee, and honey on Mondays;
among the thousand sacrifices, one should perform ten times more than the others.
Then the wise one, with a propitious mind, should offer thirty oblations for each of the thirty [deities],
and thereafter perform twenty-five oblations for the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
The knower of mantras certainly becomes established [in his station] by means of the Śiva-mantra;
thereafter, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), having offered oblations five times with all the mantras, [attains the fruit]. (55)
Having made a total renunciation of everything in that [state], one should cause his state of being a monk (*bhikṣutva*) to be offered as a sacrifice with all the mantras, once each. 56.
Having purified it of further defilement, one should unite it with the world of Brahmā;
then, having performed the reconnection as before, one should break it open once again.

Having worshipped the gods as before, one who knows the ritual procedure should undertake the previously mentioned method; [thereby] he attains the state of Brahmā, the state of Vāsudeva, or the state of Rudra. (58)
With a well-concentrated mind, one should perform the fire-oblation through the yoga of ritual action as before;
having split the cauldron as previously described, [one worships] the petals, Rudra, and the lords of the directions.
One should worship Brahmā on the crown according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should station Agni and Rudra in their own place, Kāla in the south,
Bhayānaka in the southwest, and the mighty Vāruṇa in the west.
Having assigned Śoṣaṇa to the western quarter and Kāmarūpa to the north,
one should then appoint Rudra, the lord of all vidyās, to the northeastern quarter.
One should worship all [the deities] with their own mantras, and Śambhu, the Lord, like Śiva;
having prepared the maṇḍala and performed the libation according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Then, having generated the state of Śambhu as Rudra, one should cause opposition;
for the remaining [deities], one should offer expiation with twenty oblations each in successive order.
The earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) is to be purified; one should then join it with Varuṇa.
Likewise, fire (tejas) [is joined] with Vāyu, and I [am joined] with the quality that delights in play (krīḍiṣaṇa-guṇa). (65)
In the *prakṛti* and in the *puruṣa*, as well as in *rāga*, *vidyā*, and *kala*;
then in *kāla*, again in *māyā*, and likewise in *vidyā* and *īśvara*. (66)
Likewise, in the principle of Sadāśiva, and similarly in the Sakala-niṣkala [state],
one should contemplate the attributes of the lords of all principles, as well as other attributes of the principles.
Having purified [the self] by this rite, one should place it in the Unmanī state within the causal [principle].
Then, one should worship the one supreme Śiva within all the principles (tattvas).

One should perform the installation of all the constituent principles (tattvas) with their respective mantras; then, upon that very image of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should sequentially assign the lords of those principles.
One should place that [deity] in the center and assign those Rudras in their respective positions;
as before, one should perform all rites and traverse all paths.
O Six-faced One, the procedure for the state of unmanī at the end of the oblation is likewise declared to be fourfold;
now listen regarding the body.
One becomes pure through the purification by the cow; of this there is no doubt in this world—by means of the previously mentioned procedure and by the five concentrations (dhāraṇās). || 72 ||
One should again purify all the principles (tattvas) residing within the body by means of the *ṇa* syllable;
first, one should unite the bound soul (*paśu*) with Śiva according to the previously stated procedure.
When the rite has been performed within the sphere of authority that transcends Śiva, which is as pure as clear crystal, the purification of Śiva is prescribed for him alone.

Having consecrated it seven times with mantras, one should join the scissors with the *kṣurikā* weapon-mantra at the location of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), provided it has been treated with the three sweets (*trimadhura*). (75)
The knower of mantras should deposit [the seed] with the *śivabīja* ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
he should then unite it with the causal principle situated in the midst of the enclosure of the *śakti*.
Thereafter, one should release [the soul] from its office by means of the Anamaska [mantra].
Then, preceded by the mantra and the deity, one should perform the rite intended for that specific person.

O Six-faced One, that which is performed according to the prescriptions seen in the ritual scriptures will certainly yield its fruit; however, that which is done according to one's own whims is devoid of efficacy.
By that action, one attains neither accomplishment, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal. || 79 ||
Thus ends the chapter on initiation in the Kriyāpāda of the Sarvajñānottara.
I shall now briefly state the definitive procedure for initiation,
as taught by the Supreme Lord for the benefit of the four social classes.
Having withdrawn all the principles (tattvas), one should transform them fivefold;
then, once again, the deities and the mantras within them [should be arranged] in their proper order.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—these five elements indeed pervade all things. (3)
The binding of the body is not established without the five principles;
having understood them through their gross and subtle divisions, one should purify them.
O Six-faced One, all principles (tattvas) are pure;
and through the pure deities, all the gods indeed become remembered as pure.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Ananteśa, and Sadāśiva are traditionally known as the presiding deities of the principles (tattvas), beginning with earth, respectively. (6)
Among them, let the middle mantra be the one called Vibhīta;
the thirty-third belongs to Śambhu, while the others have no specific name.
Having performed the preliminary rite, one should likewise fashion the womb;
there is no further grasping, nor likewise the joining with a sacrificial animal.
The supreme practitioner should accomplish [the rite] with the Nivṛtti mantra;
he should perform the consecration with the Guhyaka mantra and offer the oblation with the Vidyāghora mantra.
The practitioner should know that one hundred oblations for each [deity] are to be offered with the *puruṣa* mantra for Śānti, and with the *śiva* mantra for Śāntyatītā. || 10 ||
And by these very oblations, animals are indeed liberated from the bondage of birth;
likewise, [the rites of] Garbhādhāna, Puṃsavana, and Sīmantonnayana [are accomplished]. || 11 ||
One who knows the ritual procedures [should perform] the birth, the renunciation, the first feeding of solid food, as well as the investiture with authority, the enjoyment, and the dissolution.
And then [he taught] the purification of the stream, the complete purification of the principles (tattva), as well as disjunction, extraction, and the reconnection of the principles. || 13 ||
One should perform cutting, piercing, and burning upon these as previously described;
thereafter, one should effect the purification into the stainless state within the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth.
As before, one should lead the principles (tattvas) conjoined with the body to Śiva;
I shall now further proclaim this supreme secret, more secret than the secret. (15)
Free from mental impressions, having shattered his karma and being solely devoted to yoga, he worshipped the tranquil god Śiva and the palace of him who possesses immeasurable splendor. (16)

O Six-faced One, one should again perform a thousand-fold oblation with the Brahma-mantras and their limbs; furthermore, O Six-faced One, having offered another eight thousand oblations to the God, [one should proceed].
Having withdrawn the person (pudgala), one should afterwards join it before Śiva;
then, having reconstituted the principles (tattvas), one should again dissolve them with the root mantra.

Then, by that very same path, one should join [the mind] to the reality of the *bindu*, O Six-faced One, so that it becomes "mindless" (*amanaska*), just as the reality of *vāsa* was previously described. (19)
Having made them adhere to the body, one should again apply them to that reality; having joined the bound soul (paśu) with Śiva according to the previously stated procedure.
And likewise, if Śivā, having performed this, should effect freedom from ailment,
then the initiation and the sacrifice of Caṇḍeśvara are equal in this way.
Having first performed the sacrifice for the Guru, on the following day, the spiritual son (putraka) [should proceed].
The Guru, too, having purified himself, should worship the Deity of Knowledge according to the prescribed rule;
then, this one whose self is known as Śiva should proceed again to the lineage of Gurus.
On the western side of the Lord's mandala, according to the path taught in the scriptures,
those whose minds were joyful worshipped the lotus-seated one with the Ajanya-mantra.
[He worshipped] Sadāśiva and Ananta, Vidyārudra together with Umā, Viṣṇu the Lord of Gods, Brahmā, and Skanda as well. || 25 ||
Thereafter, the spiritual son (putraka), having performed the *samayika* rite, should worship Śambhu as well as the Guru with perfumes, flowers, oblations, garments, ornaments, and vehicles. (26)
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should likewise offer oneself [to the deity].
Thus, having offered oneself, one is liberated from the bonds of the guru. (27)
"From this moment forth, O Blessed One, that bodiless self of mine which belongs to you shall always be praised by you through your conceptualization as a child. (28)
Thus, remaining under the authority of the guru and being content for as long as life lasts, when permitted by him, the one of excellent vows may perform his duties. (29)
One should know that the fire-ritual, recitation, worship, initiation,
sacred knowledge, and vows are all in vain for those whose teacher is not their deity.
"The guru is the father, the guru is the mother, the guru is the deity, the guru is the friend;
there is nothing higher than the guru—thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śiva. (31)
With divine knowledge and wisdom, he opens the eyes that were overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance; therefore, he is indeed composed of knowledge.
They attain the states of perfected beings, Vidyādharas, enjoyments, and the realms of gods, asuras, and humans, by means of the ritual action prescribed by the Guru.
By the path instructed by the Guru, they attain the supreme state;
therefore, the Guru is proclaimed first, and afterwards the stainless God.
Since initiation leads one to supreme, eternal knowledge,
therefore, O Guha, nothing further than the gurus needs to be understood there.
By him the gurus have been gratified along with me and the hosts of Rudras;
there is no doubt that the gods, together with Indra, have likewise been gratified.
(88) Through contempt and anger, falling into hell is certain;
therefore, having understood this, one must never treat the Guru with disrespect. || 37 ||
One should not mount a seat, a bed, or a vehicle in the presence of one's guru.

(One should not engage in teaching: Sitting on a lower seat than the guru, he should remain standing and devoted to him; he must never wear a variegated garment, a turban, or sandals in his presence. (39)
One should not wear a crown or other blazing ornaments in the presence of the Guru;
nor should one engage in teaching, exposition, or the gathering of disciples. (40)
Staying in the presence of the guru, one should provide instruction to the guru’s disciples;
likewise, one must not listen to censure of the guru nor to censure of the scriptures. (41)
O Six-faced One, one should not transgress against the King, the preceptors, the sages, the Guru, or one's own brother, whether he be the elder or the younger. || 42 ||
Likewise, O Guruśiva, one should always regard all those who are senior to oneself;
never, under any circumstances, should a younger person [be placed above] one who is senior by virtue of initiation or consecration.
Even for one who is superior in austerity and knowledge, there must be no showing of contempt;
those who have been previously initiated by others are to be known as gurus in every respect. (44)
O Six-faced One, those others are always to be honored and worshipped as gurus.
Thus ends the chapter on initiation concerning the principles of *kalā* and the five *tattvas* in the *Kriyāpāda* of the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*.
Even if one has received the supreme initiation and has diligently partaken of the food offered by the guru, if he remains within [the cycle] for a long time, how can there be liberation for him? (1)
What defilement can there be for one who has set out toward liberation?
Is there any action whatsoever that serves as a means for his attainment of Dharma and liberation? (2)
O Skanda, for one who is devoted to the guru, peaceful, of truthful conduct, and firm in his vows—
even for one who is deceased— the rite of initiation is prescribed as excellent.
Even for an eon, one whose mind is concentrated may practice with a single-pointed thought. || 4 ||

Having recited the principles (tattvas), the deities, and the seed-syllables, the practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual placement with *karavīra* buds and *darbha* grass upon the sacrificial altar that has been prepared.
Having bathed [the image] with the weapon-bīja using the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and auspicious water,
and having established it on the right side, one should place its name upon the heart.

Alternatively, O Six-faced One, having consecrated a space in the sky with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using mantras and having fashioned [the form] there with cow dung, one should install it therein.
O Six-faced One, within these [energies] reside the three powers, as well as dharma and adharma;
having made that very [reality] the object of focus, one should withdraw it from there and perform the oblation.

Then, having brought [the consciousness] down to the head, one should deposit all the principles (tattvas) as far as the soles of the feet; however, O gods, this is done by means of the principles, not in sequential order.
One should place the *bindu* in the principle (*tattva*) at the crown of the head; there, one should apply the *bindu*.
Having meditated upon Peace (*śānti*) in the partless state (*niṣkala*), one should [place] all [the others] from the mouth downward.
Then, one should place the god Sadāśiva above the head and the top of the section;
there, one should place the circle of Śaktis merged within his [the deity's] chest.
The practitioner of mantra should apply the Vidyā there on the tongue in the middle of the mouth;
and the eight Vidyeśvaras upon the neck and the joints of the arms.
One should place Māyā on the left side and Kāla on the right; having established Kalā upon the chest, one should place Nīlalohita in the heart. (13)

Furthermore, in that very place, another knowledge (vidyā) is traditionally taught as being the Person (puruṣa); passion (rāga), moreover, is its coloring agent, characterized by the awakening of knowledge. 14.
Having meditated on the Unmanifest within the belly, one should place the subtle elements at the navel:
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
Having placed the Guṇa (the Unmanifest) upon the spinal column, one should place the three Puruṣas in that very spot;
the Intellect (Buddhi) and the Ego (Ahaṅkāra) are in the space between the navel and the penis, and the elements are in the joints.
One should place the god Vyomeśvara, the Lord of Space, in the middle of space;
right there, one should join Vāyu, who is surrounded by the eight secret secrets.
Within the generative organ, one should place the Fire element (Hutāśana) at the location of the anus;
below that, the Water element (Vāruṇa-tattva) extends as far as the kneecaps.
Within that [space], as far as the two *āmūṣlaka* pegs, one should place the worlds;
and at the beginning of the worlds, one should install the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
O Guha, one should contemplate the seven netherworlds and hells situated at the base of the ankle, slightly inward from its edge.
Having established the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign Master of Time, upon the big toe according to the prescribed rite, one should worship him again in due order.
Having brought them together and reflected upon them, the knower of mantras, beginning from the feet up to the head, should purify them by placing them all upon his shoulders.
Having performed the sacrifice as is appropriate, having fashioned the womb in the reality (tattva) according to the sequence,
and having gathered the victim as before, one should unite it. (23)
Having performed all the rites starting from the *garbhādhāna* as before,
one should likewise unite [the soul] with Śiva within all the *tattvas*.
Having placed the effigy, which is mixed with milk, clarified butter, and curd, upon the point of a needle,
the wise man should subsequently offer it as an oblation into the fire.
Alternatively, again, one should join the five elements—ether, air, fire, water, and earth—in this way, according to their gross and subtle distinctions. (26)
O Six-faced One, one should place all those [elements] within them because they consist of the principles (tattvas);
and they are pervaded by the digits (kalās), such as Śānti, Śaṅkara, and so forth, in due order.
The supreme Bindu-ākāśa is pervaded by the Śūnyā-kalā;
the Sadāśiva-tattva is pervaded by the Śāntā-kalā, which has the form of air.
Its manifest state is the very foot of that knowledge which consists of light;
and it is pervaded by its established state, from the unmanifest up to the waters.
And afterwards, he emitted the cosmic egg, both external and internal;
it was pervaded by the Rudras and filled with a terrifying roar.
That which is pervaded by emptiness is itself called "empty. Wind is pervaded by the wind-element, and fire is pervaded by the fire-element. (31)
The waters are said to be [governed] by Vāruṇī, and the broad earth is encompassed by Pārthivī;
that which lies between them and how it is pervaded is designated by their names. || 32 ||
Thus, the pervasion (vyāpti) exists externally; in reality, it resides within the body.
And this sequence of purification is established by relying upon the bound soul (paśu). (33)
Having intentionally visualized the form as before, one should likewise contemplate the channels;
O Six-faced One, one should then install the three powers, as well as merit and demerit.
Endowed with the five subtle elements and enveloped by the three qualities,
the person (pudgala) resides in the heart along with the mind, intellect, ego, and the unmanifest.
One should place Śrī and Īśā above the ears and between the eyebrows;
below that, in the heart, and above that, in the navel, one should likewise place Śānti.
One should join the Vidyā-śakti with the radiant energy (tejas) from the heart down to the genitals;
one should install the Varuṇa-pratiṣṭhā from below the genitals as far as the knees.
Below that, one should apply the earthly principle as far as the soles of the feet;
having meditated there, one should perform the rite of cessation (nivṛtti) and worship as before. || 38 ||

One should assign that seed-syllable which is the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara) according to the tradition of the Kalās; then again, the limbs of Śiva beginning with the armor (kavaca) and ending with the head (śiraḥ), as well as the Śaktis, in their proper order.
Those principles (tattvas), beginning with space (ākāśa) and ending with earth (pṛthivī), are recorded as being conjoined with the elements of earth, water, seed (fire), energy, air, and self.

Those five breaths beginning with the short [vowels], excluding the neuter ones, are to be known by the best of teachers as residing in the subtle elements (tanmātras), such as smell and the rest. || 41 ||
Ego (ahaṃkāra) is indeed the name [of the letter A], while the ocean is the name [of the letter U];
the letter M is said to be the mind (manas), and it is proclaimed to be darkness (tamas). || 42 ||
Know that the letter *ra* is *rajas*, while *saṃsattva* is proclaimed [to be the letter *sa*]. O Skanda, one should purify the letter *ya* by conceptualizing it as *prakṛti*. (43)
One should purify the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth by means of [the mantras] Nivṛtti and the others;
likewise, one should purify the five subtle elements beginning with smell by means of Sadyojāta and the others, in due order.

The knower of the ritual procedure, having mastered the fire-sacrifice, should offer ego and the other [principles] in sequence according to the threefold truth (tritatva), and with the *praṇava*, he should offer the three qualities (*guṇatraya*).

In each respective principle (tattva), however, the knower of principles should purify the five subtle elements, as well as the three qualities (guṇas), the manifest (vyakta), and the mind, intellect, and ego. (46)
One should offer one hundred oblations for each [deity] with pure clarified butter,
or with sesame seeds mixed with ghee, or with rice grains combined with clarified butter.

Then one should perform the oblation with bilva fruits, bilva leaves, or auspicious flowers offered in the arghya-vessel; and with those same materials, one should likewise offer the desired final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
As before, however, there is purification of the channels through the complete purification of the principles;
having sequentially united with the principles and abandoned them by means of that [purification], one should lead [the soul] to Śiva. (51)
Thus, O Six-faced One, initiation has been described for one who is dead; indeed, even for one who is living, being liberated from the rules and so forth, he is easily released from bondage. (50)
According to the principle of emanation and reabsorption, the conceptualization of the sounds is distinct;
initiation should be performed through reabsorption, as is agreed upon by both [traditions]. (51)
When one has failed, all ritual action is destroyed; it is completed in a single [act].
O Skanda, this is the established practice for the sake of achieving success in life.
Thus ends the chapter on the initiation of the deceased in the Kriyāpāda of the Sarvajñānottara.
Now, O Six-faced One, I shall further explain how an embodied being who has violated the conduct of the observance (samayācāra) becomes purified when he has met with calamity.

Having thoroughly cleansed it with earth and water consecrated by the recitation of the Astra-mantra, the knower of mantras should smear it with pure *āmalaka* fruits and establish it with auspicious water.
Having performed the ash-bath in reverse order, one should cause [the disciple] to circumambulate;
having adorned him with perfumes and flowers, one should place his feet in water.
One should offer [the deity] with red perfumes, flowers, unhusked grains, garments, and sacred threads;
and, accompanied by new clothing and the recitation of mantras, one should raise [the image].
Having performed the initiation of Śaṅkarī, one should place her in a pure location;
there, one should designate a sacred field (śivakṣetra) for the ritual bathing of Nirṛti. || 5 ||
It should be four cubits long, two cubits deep, and equal in width;
it is to be staked outside at the intermediate directions with stakes consecrated by the recitation of the Astra-mantra.
One should wrap it in reverse order with a red thread called *kavaca*;
then, one should draw the mandala there with yellow powder in its center.
It should be joined with three stages, and likewise a *śṛṅgāṭaka* (crossroads) above;
it should be made with red powder or with all kinds of grains.
One should establish the fire there according to the previously mentioned procedure;
with the Astra-mantra, one should spread the darbha-grass seats in the reverse order for the deities.
One should likewise perform the sprinkling around and the sprinkling with the firebrand;
at the conclusion of the oblation, one should place the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles upon the corpse.
(95) One should cause the clarified butter to be offered as before, having turned it back in reverse order; likewise, O Six-faced One, one should perform the opening and the final conclusion.
Having thus gratified the fire and offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should then install the Mantra-siṃhāsana in reverse order, beginning with sovereignty (aiśvarya) and so forth.
O Guha, having performed the placement of mantras (vinyāsa) for the twilight rites and so forth upon the bodies [of the deities],
and likewise upon Śiva and the auspicious seat, one should then perform the fire sacrifice (homa).

Having thus worshipped according to the rule with perfumes, flowers, purifying substances, and offerings such as water for the guest and water for the feet, the wise ones should do so according to their capacity.
Then one should contemplate the channels (nāḍīs), which are divine in form and beautiful;
thereafter, one should smear that [area] with sandalwood, agallochum, and other such substances.
O Six-faced One, his dwelling shall become his excellent house;
then, O Six-faced One, one should again sprinkle the deceased with the *mā* seed-syllable.
One should apply a cloth soaked in ghee to the middle of the fire;
then the wise practitioner should contemplate the channel within that body.
Having established one's own consciousness within the heart, the knower of mantras should place that person in the center;
then, beginning from the feet, he should contemplate the principles (tattvas).
Having thus abandoned that [earth], the knower of the ground should unite the sacrificial animal with Śivā;
there, he should kindle the fire and circumambulate it from left to right.
O Rāma, the knower of mantras should meditate upon the fire-weapon with the seed-syllable of the weapon;
likewise, he should offer unbroken oblations consecrated with the weapon-mantra.
Having whirled it with the seed-syllable of the weapon (*astrabīja*), one should cause a stream of water to descend.
Then the wise man, having bathed and offered water, should become pure. (21)
Having performed the sacrifice as prescribed and having offered it, one should ask the Lord for forgiveness;
in this way, the embodied soul is liberated from the transgression of the rules and other obligations.
"Whether performed out of ignorance or knowledge, you [are the witness] in those rites concerning the deceased.
Thus ends the section on the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*.
Thus, O Śaṅkara, you have explained initiation even for the deceased;
likewise, the funeral rite that purifies the bonds is performed even for those devoid of proper conduct.
Tell me, what is the destiny of those lifelong celibates who have conquered their selves, even though they are endowed with the practice of knowledge, yet remain without a teacher?
Through the two practices of knowledge, the two types of Buddhists shall attain the reality of the intellect;
those who are devoted to the Jina attain that which is characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*).
For those who have not conquered their own selves, liberation comes through initiation;
O Six-faced One, they behold these places of liberation.
There shall be a single place of liberation, pure and facing in all directions;
it is immovable, a dwelling place, peaceful, and free from dependence on a *liṅga*.
In that [rite], having purified the mantra of application according to the sequence of the principles (tattvas),
one should first worship the bearer of the sectarian mark (liṅgin) who is established therein.
Having thus properly performed the libations, one should purify oneself through expiation;
O Six-faced One, having spent five nights or three nights [in this manner].
Afterwards, one should perform eight thousand oblations with the weapon-bīja;
again, one should perform eight thousand oblations with the root-mantra. (8)
Having become one who has performed the supreme rite of initiation, she is the savior from the ocean of worldly existence;
indeed, the lifelong initiate remains so even through constant ritual practice.
He should always be devoted to the Śiva scriptures, intent on the fire-oblation to Śiva, pure, a worshiper of Śiva, a meditator on Śiva, and a reciter of the praises of Śiva at all times.
O Skanda, he will bestow grace upon those who have doubts;
in the Śiva tradition, there are only two types of ascetics: the householder and the celibate student. || 11 ||
Indeed, these two—the wandering mendicant and the ascetic—are the ones who perform the favoring of the worlds;
such is their authority over this task until they transfer it elsewhere.
But one whose office has been transferred should perform his duties while remaining free from karmic attachment;
his status as a householder or a celibate student is merely a matter of designation. (13)
From the ultimate perspective, neither the stages of life nor the activities of those stages exist for them;
for they have been appointed to the supreme state by means of the actions performed for that purpose.

For that purpose, no specific stage of life (āśrama) has been prescribed for one who relies upon the Śiva-śāstra; rather, he should perform the morning twilight recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and whatever rites have come down through tradition. 15.
One who is constantly devoted to the mantra should perform some practice for the sake of stability;
for in that [mantra] the embodied soul, having received initiation, abides as one whose nature is Śiva.

Remaining constantly established in that very state, one should practice the Śiva-dharma; O Six-faced One, whatever has been taught in this Śiva-śāstra regarding prescribed action [is to be followed]. (17)

Therefore, that transgression must certainly be performed; having bypassed it, this is to be known as the Command (ājñā), to be known as the Cause (kāraṇa), and never to be conceptualized otherwise. (18)
When [a matter] is established, there is no means of proof (*sādhana*) and no refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) exists;
for the word of a human seer (*ṛṣi*) is not authoritative, nor is that of a divine seer (*devarṣi*). (19)
Neither by the gods is the word of a Brahmin ever contradicted, nor is the word of Viṣṇu contradicted by the Lotus-born Brahmā, nor is the word of Śiva ever contradicted by Viṣṇu. (20)
Whosoever oppresses them is a deluded soul, utterly ruined and of foolish intellect; for it is proclaimed that among all these, each succeeding one is superior to the preceding. (21)
The wise who understand the meaning of statements, as well as those seeking the welfare [of others],
should not disregard the ten rites that are well-known through their connection [to the Vedic texts] and are intended for the benefit of the person,
beginning from the rite of impregnation (garbhādhāna) up until the final bath (udvāha). || 23 ||
O Skanda, one should perform the occasional rites first and the regular ones afterwards, as they appear in sequence; one should not practice worldly duties by neglecting the primary ones.
One should not honor another teacher nor remember another deity;
being endowed with pure meditation, one's mind should be directed solely toward Śiva. (25)
One shall attain the pure state that is inconceivable, all-pervading, and eternal;
whereas that which is variegated, characterized by doubt regarding karma, and produced by what has been done, arises from volitional action.
The fruit of that mantra will not bring happiness here or in the solitary state;
rather, one should resort to pure action when it has been attained according to one's desire.
One who is always devoted to that action becomes happy through it;
99) with his senses conquered, he performs pure actions without contradicting the scripture itself. || 28 ||
By this very body one attains success; there is no doubt about this.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even those of impure birth may be practitioners. (29)
O Six-faced One, the preceptors, beginning with Suvarṇādāna, were faithful and free from envy; they were knowers of action and devoted to their duties.
Those who are devoted and attached to you are remembered as your benefactors;
O Six-faced One, wherever the black-colored deer roams, [that place is sacred].
One should know that region to be fit for sacrifice which is inhabited by Brahmins, where there are Brahmins of virtuous conduct and ascetics whose wealth is their austerity. (32)
One should designate him as having a meritorious body, along with the gods and the Vedas;
the teachers born in that region and lineage should be in accordance with the scriptures.
Devoted to the Śiva-śāstra, the supreme and eternal, and dedicated to the worship of Śiva and the sacred fire,
the twice-born indeed performs the ash-bath from head to foot.
Above the navel, it is prescribed for the Brahmin that there be a line made with ash;
for the Vaiśya, a broad stripe is prescribed, while for the Śūdra, the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) is ordained.
With ashes consecrated by the Brahma-mantra applied to the respective places in due order,
the matted locks of a Brāhmaṇa are proclaimed to be like golden ones.
The intermediate [intervals] for a Kṣatriya should be known as twice that [of the Brāhmaṇa];
one lock of hair is prescribed in its place for a Vaiśya, and likewise for a Śūdra. (37)

For a self-controlled man who has conquered his senses, the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) of a Brahmin should be short, smooth, joined [with strands], made of five threads, and [worn] with the sacred cord placed over the left shoulder. (38)
It is said that for a Kṣatriya there are three syllables; for a Vaiśya, it is traditionally remembered as two syllables;
and for a Śūdra who is always constant [in his duty], it should be known as one syllable. (39)
"In worship, in the fire-rite, or at the time of the twilight prayers, and not otherwise.
Thus ends the chapter on the extraction of the *liṅga* and so forth in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*.
Henceforth, I shall fully proclaim the procedure for consecration (abhiṣeka) for the benefit of the disciples, just as it issued from the mouth of Śambhu.
On the previously mentioned pure ground, smeared with cow dung, delightful with all kinds of beauties, and adorned with all fragrances; || 2 ||

On an auspicious lunar day, weekday, asterism, and moment, accompanied by a favorable *karaṇa*; when there is the rising of benefic planets in the ascendant, and it is joined with auspicious omens. || 3 ||
One who practices the vow of truth, self-controlled, endowed with renunciation, possessed of compassion, cheerful of countenance, skillful, devoted to his guru, and firm in his vows.
One who has mastered the Tantra [should accept] a disciple who is fully endowed with purity and right conduct, disciplined in yoga, with senses conquered, devoted to Śiva, and ever tranquil.
Having performed the sacrifice as prescribed and completed the initiation, the knower of mantras,
who discerns what is appropriate and inappropriate, should then consecrate him.
With lutes, flutes, mṛdaṅga drums, and the like, with trumpets, kettledrums, and other instruments, and with the sounding of conchs and horns accompanied by dance and song.
One should commence the consecration (abhiṣeka), endowed with all auspiciousness,
to the southeast, west, or north of the sacrificial site. (8)
One should fashion the navel behind the opening, and then prepare the *taṇḍula* (rice-grain shaped pedestal),
which has a width of thirty-two *aṅgulas* and a height of the same measure.
It should be square, even, and pure, adorned with a lotus in the center;
having arranged the pedestal (pīṭha) as before, one should install [the deity] therein and worship it. || 10 ||
Having bathed and adorned his body with mantras,
he should then arrange the water-pots as before, beginning from the east.

Following the procedure for the auspicious water-pot (śivakumbha) and joined with the mantra-deity, the practitioner of mantras should unite the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) with the eight [syllables]. 12.
Perform the recitation of the four limbs in their proper places, the five Brahmans in the five [locations], one [recitation] of the weapon-mantra, and likewise another of the Śiva-mantra. (13)
One should prepare a vessel made of forest materials for the purpose of sipping water with the Gāyatrī;
having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should consecrate it with the mantra named Śiva.
First, the knower of the ritual procedure, having bathed [the deity] with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra),
should then [bathe him] with the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), beginning with Ananta, in their proper order.
Then, O Six-faced One, Śiva himself should perform the consecration again in due order with the Brahma-mantras, following the sequence of the limbs.
Then, having honored [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, garments, ornaments, sandals,
the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), purifiers (*pavitra*), and so forth, one should offer a silken cloth (*paṭṭa*) upon the ground.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the preceptor, accompanied by Śiva,
should approach the presence of Śiva and formally surrender the authority. (18)
"O Lord of Yogis, that authority which was entrusted to me by my Guru like a calf to its mother has, from this day forward, been transferred by me to you. (19)
Likewise, disciples are to be favored by means of the rites prescribed in the scriptures;
the Śiva-scripture is to be heard, and it should be taught to those who seek it.
When the disciple has resided [as a student] for one year, the wise teacher should perform the initiation;
he should bestow the initiation into the mantra upon that reality (tattva) in which he is consecrated.
Having offered oblations into the other [fires], one should fashion the Hand of Śiva;
thereafter, one should likewise rub the Samayas and the limbs of Brahmā.
One must not criticize the Lord who is the cause, nor that scripture originating from Śiva, nor the preceptor, nor the spiritual son; one must never transgress the word of the Guru.

O Lord, a wise man should carefully avoid contact with a woman who has recently given birth, as well as her shadow for a distance of four cubits; he should also avoid meat that has been eaten by a butcher’s dog.
Thus, these commitments have been briefly proclaimed according to the tantras;
by them, guardians attain Śiva, but otherwise, they meet with total obstruction. (25)
The Piṇḍa-mantra consists of three syllables, and Śiva is the soul of the year;
this knowledge should be given to those who know the samaya, but one should not bestow it upon anyone else.

Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, Śūdras, and others, including those of indeterminate gender—these are not to be scrutinized at the time of initiation; however, one should exercise discernment regarding the bestowal of knowledge.
O Brahmin, one should cause a Kṣatriya to pay with three, four, or five [units]; a Vaiśya with nine, seven, or eight; and a Śūdra with ten or twenty. (28)
O Guha, this essence of the Śiva-śāstra, the most excellent of all scriptures and more secret than the secret, must be preserved with great effort.
It should not be given to a non-disciple, nor to one who lacks devotion, nor to an atheist,
nor to one who hates the guru, nor to one who delights in inferior scriptures.
O Six-faced One, he who possesses supreme and constant devotion toward the God and the Guru, but lacks such devotion toward other scriptures, he shall not be joined with that knowledge.
One should never engage in verbal dispute regarding the Śiva-scriptures,
nor should one cause any obstruction to the ten classes of people.
In a secluded, uninhabited, and beautiful place, one who has conquered the senses, is pure, and has bathed should cause the Guru—the worshipful Lord of Knowledge—to proclaim the Śiva-jñāna. || 33 ||

And it should be heard by those who are such [as described], who are capable, and who have that as their ultimate goal; having joined with the Guru at the beginning and the end, they should honor him with purified minds. (34)
One should not teach the Śivajñāna on the full moon day, the new moon day, on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, during eclipses, or at the junctions of the seasons.
O Six-faced One, one should perform the recitation, worship, vow, and fire-offering with special care; among all these, [one should excel] through generosity, fasting, and self-restraint. (36)
Ungrateful, atheistic, cruel, devoid of truth, fond of quarreling,
possessed of deceit and guile— such are those who will seize the Tantras at the end of the age.
Whether they inquire with sweet words or address Śeṣa again,
one who desires peace for oneself should not place trust in them. (38)
Thus, indeed, as long as the authority over ritual action has not been transferred elsewhere, one who has transferred that authority should practice the renunciation of karma (saṃnyāsa). || 39 ||
O child, the consecration of the practitioner (sādhaka) is performed in this manner;
both the preceptor (ācārya) and the practitioner possess equal auspiciousness. (40)

Once his learning is complete, the teacher should be treated as an accomplished practitioner (sādhaka). He is to be known as one who possesses both desire and the arrow; he is remembered by me as the preceptor (deśika) who represents the ultimate goal.
The single ritual procedure for both the manifestation and the dissolution of existence is always performed by the Guru through a small amount of oblation, recitation, and meditation. (42)
"For the best of practitioners is always firmly established in the perfection of ritual action.
Thus ends the chapter on consecration in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrī-Sarvajñānottara.
Hereafter, I shall explain the ritual bathing according to the rules for the Brahmins,
performed either with five jars prepared according to the previously mentioned procedure.
The practitioner of mantra should assign the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) to one [part],
the five Brahmās to the second, and the four limbs to the third.
Let it be; the fourth [vessel] is the Śiva-kumbha, and there is a fifth. Having consecrated them with mantras according to the prescribed placement (nyāsa), one should perform the bath as before.
The knower of mantras should perform the consecration with four jars as prescribed;
first, with the [mantra] beginning with Vidyeśvara, and then with the Brahma-aṅgas.
The third [vessel] should be joined with a single jar equipped with the weapon-mantra;
the fourth, the Śiva-jar, one should consecrate as before. (5)
Alternatively, one should prepare two jars for the consecration:
in one [should be placed] all the mantras, and the third is the jar of Śiva.
One should perform the consecration using either the leaf-cups of the *brahmapatra* tree, or else with conch-shells or mother-of-pearl; thereafter, one should again request permission.
Whether with flowers, or even with the mind, or even with speech, one may offer praise;
however, without being authorized by the mantra, one should not perform the ritual of the mātrikās.
Then, having gathered the ladle and the rosary in their proper order,
one should perform worship, recitation, and fire-offerings at the three times of day.
Thus ends the section on the abbreviated consecration in the Kriyāpāda of the Sarvajñānottara.
Listen to the true procedure for the *sruva* ladle and the *avakṣa*-thread;
I shall now describe, in due order, the substances for the accomplishment of *japa*.
The *sruva* spoon should be one cubit in length, while the *āghāra* ladle is the size of the thumb’s joint;
the *sruk* ladle should be known to be one forearm in length, with its bowl resembling the palm of the hand.
Having washed a staff made of *pālāśa*, *aśvattha*, *bilva*, or *vikaṅkata* wood with the weapon-mantra (*astrabīja*), one should purify it through meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*).
Then, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and again with scented water,
one should join the three principles (tritatva) and the seed-syllable of Śakti to both [the disciple and the image].
Having adorned [the deity] with perfumes and flowers, one who knows the ritual procedure should offer incense;
having maintained the presence for seven nights, he should thereafter perform the fire oblation (homa).
Having gone to the Madhu tree, one should purify the fruit of the Putra-dīpa;
cow dung from the Khasa region should be taken and smeared there once again. (6)
The mantra-practitioner should sprinkle [the tree] as before with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra and auspicious perfumes;
having thus made that tree "Śiva-like," he should worship it just like Śiva himself.
Having first performed the fire-ritual according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures,
and having offered the bali-oblation to the spirits, one should thereafter withdraw the senses.
Śiva should recite the mantra produced from the middle branch;
O Skanda, born from the eastern branch, one should mutter the Tatpuruṣa [mantra] at the opening of the cave.
Or [one may worship] Aghora and Vāmadeva, or even Sadyojāta and Aṅga;
one should conceive of them as being praised by whichever mantras are present according to their actual state.
Those belonging to Vāyu, Anala, Mahendra, Varuṇa, and those that are mixed—with these akṣas born from their respective streams, all achieve success without a doubt. (11)
One should fashion a rosary for a maiden using a triple-stranded thread, not one that is tripled again;
it should be made of pure *akṣa* seeds with water from a sacred weapon-mantra.
Whether one hundred and eight, or fifty-four, or twenty-seven—the rosary used by the practitioner of mantra is declared to be auspicious. (13)
Having first performed the placement of the powers (śaktinyāsa), one should deposit it upon that thread;
one should pierce it with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astrabīja) and string it together with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Having placed them together with their openings facing one another and well-compressed, they expel pure breaths that are free from obstruction, undivided, stainless, and devoid of defects. || 15 ||
Then, having washed it with auspicious water, one should adorn it again with perfumes.
One should place the Śakti in its own stream, and likewise the Vīrapatra upon it. (16)

Having covered [the animal] with peacock feathers and crescent-shaped ornaments, one should subsequently apply the axle-fastenings; likewise, perform the ritual slaughter after the hero's leaf has been applied.
There, one should worship one's own mantra with perfumes and flowers in due order; having thus made that thread identical with Śiva, one should wrap it up day after day.
Then the mantra-practitioner should cause it to be placed in a casket that has been consecrated with mantras—
whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, or even iron.
