One who knows the ritual procedure should perform the seizing, the releasing, and the establishing;
furthermore, the worship and the anointing should be performed within the heart.
Therefore, I shall further describe briefly the supreme procedure for the dice:
having procured skillful dice, one should [mark them] with ashes consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra.
The one skilled in *dhāraṇā* should then perform purification in sequence with water mixed [with the five products],
and thereafter with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and again with scented water.
Then, having washed it with auspicious water, one should adorn it again with perfumes;
and having performed the sacrifice as prescribed, according to the previously mentioned method regarding the girdle.

Then, having drawn the collection of vital breaths into the circle of the heart and becoming centered within the three principles (tritatva), one should perform the recitation with a concentrated mind.
Standing between the three sacred sites (tritattva), one should perform the recitation with a concentrated mind,
using three handfuls of water daily until the prescribed number is completed.
p.
108) First, one should offer the recitation (japa) to Śiva with scented water;
having performed the recitation and performed the ritual purification (udikṣa), one should again propitiate the Lord. || 26 ||
Having drawn that [image] forth, one should likewise perform the ritual here with the vows and mantras. || 27 ||
Thus ends the chapter on recitation and related practices in the Kriyāpāda of the venerable Sarvajñānottara.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme vow among all vows,
known as the Śiva-vrata, which is always honored by the gods.
His birth is pure and white; he is adorned with white garments and unguents, wears a white sacred thread, and is graced by a crown of matted locks. || 12 ||
Endowed with all ornaments and adorned with white garlands,
he became the essence of celibacy, having worshipped Śiva’s fire and his guru.
Just as the mantra-form of Śiva itself has been proclaimed as it was before, so indeed should the vow of the lords of practitioners be understood as being of that same nature. 14.
Wearing a white loincloth or garment, a turban, and carrying a rosary and a water-pot,
he should dwell constantly in the temple of Śiva, subsisting on alms and having his senses subdued.
Devoted to meditation on Śiva, observing silence, and worshipping Śiva’s fire and the Guru, he shall become equal to Śiva once a year has passed. || 16 ||
Thus ends the chapter on the Śiva-vow in the Kriyāpāda of the Sarvajñānottara.
Henceforth, I shall describe the installation of Lakṣmaṇa in the abode of Śiva,
as well as the installation of the Liṅga, in which everything is established.
All the deities, beginning with Brahmā, abide by resorting to the *liṅga*; therefore, one should indeed install the *liṅga* according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures. (2)

A yogi who has mastered the three Vedas, observes his vows, worships his guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, who is a teacher, knows reality, is wise, born of a distinguished lineage, and pure—[such a one should be honored]. (3)

O Guha, even one who lacks all auspicious marks, if he is a knower of the meaning of the Śiva scriptures, is an authorized installer (sthāpaka) as proclaimed by others and is approved by the Śiva-vijñāna scriptures. || 4 ||
One who is endowed with all the characteristics but does not find the perfect scripture is neither a yogi, nor one purified by vows, nor is he called a teacher. || 5 ||

One who is deceitful, an atheist, cruel, slanderous, or envious; one with a bad complexion, a friend of the wicked, one who is deformed, one suffering from consumption, or one with dropsy—[these are not to be accepted]. 6.
One-eyed, with squinting reddish-brown eyes, and wearing a skull as a crest—
O child, one should avoid a logician who is the abode of all defects.

One should avoid those who are professional sacrificers, those who subsist on food offered to the gods, those who observe vows for the gods, perpetual celibates, and those who perform installations, when [performing] consecrations.

Having understood the purity of the place, the purity of the self, as well as the purity of the ritual materials, and the purity of the mantra and its characteristic marks, one becomes a performer of the rite.
Then, one should sprinkle the site with the water from the Śiva-weapon (astra-mantra);
thereafter, one should again designate the field as either Māhendra or Vāruṇa.
Then one should perform the binding of the directions as previously described;
in this way, the purification of the site is accomplished, and the purification of the body is likewise enjoined.
The purification of the mantra consists of the purification of the mind; this is for the practitioner who is skilled in mantras.
Furthermore, the impurities, the powers, and the knowledges of mantras have been proclaimed. (12)
Their awakening power is the command of Śiva, not the state of being a mantra;
thus is the purification of the mantra succinctly proclaimed.
The purification of ritual objects consists in sprinkling them with the auspicious water of Śiva;
furthermore, I shall describe the purification of the liṅga and that which pertains to the worship performed at dawn.
The characteristics of the *liṅga* by which it attains presence are as follows:
the sacred field (*kṣetra*) of a *liṅga* installed by a teacher extends for one hundred cubits from the *liṅga*. || 15 ||
In the Svāyaṃbhūva [Manvantara], there shall be a thousand [years]; however, with the Ṛṣis, it is meaningful [only] when accompanied by the truth.
Having performed the purification of the ground, effect the generation of the field.
Once the auspicious site has been consecrated, the demarcation of the ground should follow;
thereafter, the knower of the ritual rules, having laid out the threads, performs the placement of the foundation stone.

Having adorned it with seeds such as gold and gems, one should deposit it amidst auspicious proclamations of "May there be well-being!", shouts of victory, and the sounding of conchs and musical instruments.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu and Vināyaka with auspicious sounds of "Bāhu," one should then offer the oblation to the quarters after having worshipped the lords of the directions.
The preceptor, together with artisans, should fashion the linga with all its characteristic marks,
while the master builder should construct the temple as prescribed and in accordance with the scriptures.
The linga may arise from the temple, or the temple itself from the linga;
it is enjoined by that very same measurement-line (sūtra) which was previously laid down.
Having again performed the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga), one should join weapon after weapon with the [mantras of] weapons.
Having bathed it with the water of the weapon-mantra, one should apply perfumes and flowers.
Having offered incense according to the prescribed ritual, one should cause [the deity] to remain for one night,
mounted upon a bed of cloth with an axe, a chisel, and a mallet. (23)
Having anointed their faces in sequence with ghee and honey,
one should recite the Astra-mantra during meditation upon entry, and recite the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having reached Mount Udaya, he should again perform the sacrifice there in due order;
having offered the oblation to the spirits (bhūtabali), he should transform his heart.
Taking up a stone for his feet, he beheld that one of gentle appearance,
who was free from blemish, pure, stainless, and beautiful to behold.
Having consecrated the weapons with mantras, perform the attainment through the Sadyojāta mantra;
do not perform worship again there, but rather carry out the ritual action.
Then, being composed of that very essence, one should perform the division into parts;
one should conceive of the eastern and northern [sections] as the head of Īśāna.
To the east of the tree, in front of the eastern side of the palace,
or wherever the entrance may be, one should arrange the mystical diagram (yantra) right there.
To the east of the central location, one should construct a temple facing west;
likewise, to the south, one should build one facing east, and to the west, one facing east.
Likewise, it may be further to the north, or to the east, or even to the west;
however, the gate should be placed in the middle, depending on the nature of the ground.
One should not make the deity face north, nor should one do so from the south;
nor should one ever make the faces [of the deity] toward the intermediate directions.
O Śikhin, for those deities who are installed otherwise [than prescribed],
there shall be famine, conflict with kings, calamities, and fears. (33)
One should make the height one-third [of the total] and the width two-thirds;
it may be square or circular, provided with a pedestal and surrounded by a wall.
Having placed the King of Mantras on the eight sides within the enclosure wall, one should construct the palaces facing outward; one must not pierce them from the interior.
[These are located] from Indra, Pāvaka, Dharmeśa, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, and Ānila.
And one should likewise establish the deities Kubera and Īśāna among them.
Durgā and Vighnavināyaka should be stationed outside at the gateway;
likewise, Nandin and Mahākāla should be stationed in front of Śiva.
Then, in the center, there is the Śivaliṅga, which may be of superior, middling, or inferior quality;
its belly is full, its sides are even, and its back and head are elevated. (38)
It was free from crookedness and supported by a base, standing firm and straight;
it was marked with the signs of the lotus, the moon, the wheel, the śrīvatsa, and the svastika. || 39 ||
One cubit, two cubits, or even three cubits is the smallest;
four cubits, five cubits, or six cubits is the middling. (40)
Seven, eight, or nine cubits is proclaimed as the best [measurement];
white, red, yellow, and black are [the colors] for the Brahmins and the others, respectively.
Heavy, unctuous, fragrant, and endowed with a beautiful sound and brilliance— such a mixture, even if composed of four parts, is suitable for consumption and shines with excellence.
Free from all thorns, devoid of all impurities,
and endowed with all auspicious marks, one should install the Śiva-liṅga. (43)
One should fashion it from auspicious gems, measuring one finger-breadth, two fingers, four fingers, eight fingers, or a span (vitasti).
A temple for the lingas made of precious gems is not prescribed;
rather, one should worship them as desired in a temple or a beautiful house. || 45 ||
Whatever the nature of Bala’s liṅga, the altar (vedī) should be made of that same material;
the dimensions of the liṅga and the altar should be understood as equal to one another. || 46 ||
It may be made of gold, silver, or even copper, and should be stainless;
in the absence of gem-studded altars, it is prescribed for liṅgas made of gems.
Having understood the east and west of the altar, as well as the characteristics of the north, one should cause the liṅga to enter the center; two parts are prescribed for the exterior.
Two parts shall be the visible [portion], and one should cause the third to enter;
this is prescribed for jeweled liṅgas, and the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed in the cavity (*suṣira*).
For among their characteristics, having carefully divided the upper portion into three equal parts, one should then discard the part above that.
In all respects it is even, excellent, with its head neither sunken nor raised,
free from all defects, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
O Six-faced One, one should fashion it as a square, then a portion in the middle as an octagon, and finally the upper part as a circle.
From the center of a perfectly pure mark made of hen’s eggs,
one should then fashion a square. || 53 ||
It should be made more fully complete in the middle, and above that it should be raised;
or one may fashion it as eight-sided, with its center having the appearance of a closed star.
He possesses a symmetrical, flawless, pure, and radiant body that is beautiful to behold;
he is as soft as a drum, worthy of being known through desire, and his form is like that of a drum.
Whether it was installed in a forest or situated in an uneven place,
one should re-install and worship the linga made of precious gems.
The altar (vedi) should be elevated toward the north and resemble the surface of a mirror;
its girdle (mekhalā) should consist of twelve parts, and the water-channel (praṇāla) should be half a part.

The definition of the authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa) and the installation and worship of those [images] made of precious gems have been declared; now hear the procedure for the others.

Then, place the *garbhagranthi* (the womb-knot) at the front of the *liṅga* and make it threefold; on the middle part, fashion the altar (*vedi*) for the sacrificial grain, which is considered equal in measure to the base-altar (*bhaktivedī*). || 59 ||
The knower of the ritual procedure should determine that measurement as the opening; for the well-levelled smaller [shrine], he should make it twice the height in width.
Then, having set aside one-sixth part, one should place the central door;
now listen as I describe how the central area should be fashioned as prescribed.
O Six-faced One, having abandoned two parts out of three from the lower portion,
one should construct the door in the middle of the upper portion.
Having set aside one part, one should arrange two parts;
one should fill that part on the ground, and the remainder [forms] the liṅga in sequence. (63)
Having made the lower altar firm, well-prepared, and extinguished,
it should be covered with well-fitted bricks as far as the area is level.
Then, construct the arrangement of the pedestal upon the uttaravedī according to the procedure seen in the scriptures, and perform all the ritual acts accordingly.
O Six-faced One, the linga, as well as the womb, devotion, the temple, and likewise that [pedestal], one should have constructed according to the measurement of the linga. (66)
The Talliṅga [is worshipped] with the Mañjarī [offering]; likewise, the Śukanāsā, Mahāsena, and the Śikhara are associated with the Liṅga.
Furthermore, one should place the *tallaiṅgika* sūtra from the center of the womb (the central axis) to both sides;
the pavilion for the *śukanāsa* (front porch) shall be half the height of the directional square.
O Six-faced One, one should insert each phallus individually from the interior of the womb; one should place two phalluses in front of Śukanāsa. 69.
Construct a roof-awning (valabhicchāndaka), or likewise one in the shape of an elephant or a lion, or even one in the form of a swan; make the *śukanāsa* (gargoyle) symmetrical.
Two liṅgas and an ardhaliṅga are for the middle [type];
two liṅgas are prescribed for the superior [type], and one should install three liṅgas for the inferior.
Alternatively, one should determine the dimensions of the temple by taking that portion which, among all the proportions, is designated for the work of the door.
Having measured it accurately with a cord, divide the *liṅga* into three parts;
let the lower portion be square, situated at the center of the earth. (73)
The third part should be increased by one-quarter and have its top slightly raised;
above that, the middle part is praised when it is of equal proportion.
The pedestal and the liṅga are said to be equal, or they may be made with two parts for the portion of the worship;
otherwise, according to one's preference, divide the space from the liṅga to the inner sanctum into nine parts.
The middle pedestal consists of eight units, beginning with its own proportionate parts; indeed, the circumference of all these sections has been proclaimed. (76)
The portion beginning with Brahmā consists of three parts combined with sixteen squares;
thus is the field measured by the kuṇḍikā, and its circumference is proclaimed.
Whichever portion of the linga’s head one should cause to be rounded, one should further arrange that same proportion for the neck (grīvā). || 78 ||
One should place the pedestal situated in the second part upon the Brahma-vedi;
the third part, endowed with the proper characteristics, should be made for the image (arcā). || 79 ||
Leaving aside one-third of the upper portion, one should extract the characteristic mark;
having marked it with a golden thread, one should carve out that form of the liṅga.
Having carved out an eight-sided shape from the center upwards and adorned it with arms,
one should subsequently smear it with honey and clarified butter.
Having laid two threads with an interval between them, one should again lead a thread through their middle;
this is remembered as the auspicious characteristic measured by the span of the middle finger.

Now, as for the characteristics: whether according to their specific marks or even deficient in their characteristics—those who are excessively tall, emaciated, or short, the deities do not take refuge in such a protector. (83)
Therefore, with every effort, one should proclaim the auspicious characteristics:
it should be smooth, well-cut, of perfect proportions, and beautiful to behold. (84)
One who possesses the proper characteristics should construct the altar, completely free from all defects;
it should be installed with great care according to the specific form of the Liṅga.
One who possesses wealth may fashion it long if his lifespan is short, or likewise short if his lifespan is long;
therefore, one should have the *liṅga* made neither too short nor too long. (86)
With a restrained waist-string, self-conquered, with a peaceful teacher who constantly mutters the mantra; || 87 ||
When the linga, the altar, and the bull appear as if already completed,
then one who is pure should bring [the deity] mounted upon a chariot yoked with cows.
Having adorned it with perfumes and flowers and offered incense, the one who knows the ritual procedure,
having performed circumambulation from the front, should cause [the image] to enter amidst various sounds.
Having led [the image] to a divine sanctuary situated in the northeastern direction,
one should cause it to rest for one night upon a prepared soft bed and seat.
There, the preceptor, being well-composed, should first perform the rite of expiation;
having performed the fire-oblation as prescribed by the rules, he should recite the Saṃhitās beginning with the Brahma-mantras.
Then, at midnight, one should cause the eight bearers of the forms— whose bodies have been made complete (sakalīkṛta), who are peaceful, and who are intent on recitation and meditation— to enter.
"O best of Brahmins, arise and prepare for me other jars filled with water, endowed with the appropriate mantras and ritual substances. (93)
Then, having raised the *liṅga*, one should bathe it with eight or more handfuls of cold water, purified by a cloth and consecrated with the *astra-mantra*. (94)
Having purified the Liṅga, the altar, and likewise the Bull by means of the Dhāraṇās,
and having bathed them with Vāruṇa mantras and adorned them, one should cause them to enter.
Having made the stone of the quadrangular heap, with three-fingered bases and girdles,
it should be marked by a cord along the same line as the quadrangular linga.
It should be very firm, free from grass, pure, twelve finger-breadths high, placed with oblations, joined together, well-stable, and properly aligned with measuring lines. || 97 ||

Having sprinkled the site with water purified by mantras, the practitioner of mantras should place the stone in the center of the Brahma-line; thereafter, perform what is prescribed by the ritual rules.
Having fashioned such a golden tortoise, one should place it upon the back;
then, all your seeds and jewels [should be placed] there again in due order. (99)
Then, having established the stone according to the ritual procedure in its center,
the wise one should install therein the Śakti, which resembles a sprout from a sprout.
One should place yellow orpiment in the east, realgar in the southeast;
one should give red arsenic in the south, and gold-ore in the southwest.
One should place vimalaka in the west and parata in the northwest;
one should apply kāsīsa in the north and place rocanā in the northeast.
The wise should fashion [the image] with red chalk (gairika) in the station of Brahmā;
it is known to be purifying, auspicious in every way, and traditionally taught to bring about prosperity.
One should place sixty types of rice in the eastern direction, dedicated to Indra;
and one should place black gram and horse gram in the southeastern direction, dedicated to Agni. (104)
One should place mung beans and chickpeas in the southern direction, and one should place black sesame seeds and white sesame seeds in the southwestern direction. (105)
One should place wheat and barley in the western direction;
and one should place millet and śyāmāka grain in the northern direction. || 106 ||
In the northeast, one should place all grains that bring about nourishment;
one should employ all minerals and all seeds in the station of Brahmā.
Furthermore, one should offer rice and niṣpāva beans to the east,
barley to the south, and millet to the north.
One should not plant seeds too deeply; rather, one should employ them for the sake of auspiciousness.
When the seeds are sown in reverse, they cause the destruction of the embrace.
Then the defects, diseases, and fears are averted;
one should then place the Aindra-vajra and the sun-crystal (sūryakānta). 110.
An indranīla gem is in the southern direction, a vaiḍūrya in the south-western quarter;
a conch shell is in the western direction, and a puṣparāga in the north-western quarter. (111)
One should place a *marataka* gem in the north,
pearls in the northeast, a *brahma-maṇi* in the station of Brahmā, and the *amṛta* gem of Vāsuki.
One should give the *lotākṣa* for the *sādhyas*, the *pulaka* gem for all [the other classes], and one should cause the *candrakānta* to be given between the *saumya* and *śāna* [planets]. 113.
If all the [other] minerals are unavailable, one should provide yellow orpiment;
if all the seeds are unavailable, one should provide the seed of the *dhava* tree. || 114 ||
If all the gems are unavailable, one should cause a single diamond to be given;
if all the metals are unavailable, one should cause a single piece of gold to be given. || 115 ||
According to those rules, one should perform the ritual in the proper places;
and one should apply some flowers and incense to that which has become barley.
Having offered incense once more, the knower of reality should then establish the liṅga; having made a central support, he should do so with that thread.
One should cause that stationary *liṅga*—which is soundless, constant, and peaceful—to move;
one should write "Salutation to the One whose Self is All" below it with a crow's feather.
In this section, one should place the Grandfather (Brahmā) of yellow color in a square;
however, in the center, one should place Puruṣottama, who resembles the flax flower (atasī-puṣpa).
One should place Rudra, who possesses a luster like that of a pure kunda flower or the moon, in the circular portion;
there, all the deities are to be worshipped, residing in their respective portions.
That which is the primordial sovereign splendor, consisting of all the gods,
and which has become a condensed mass of the principles (tattvas), is therefore called the *liṅga* by the ignorant.
One should know her as she truly is: possessing a luster like pure gold, the mother of the Gaṇas, Ambikā, the meritorious nurse, the primordial mistress of yogis. 122.

Having placed the feet [of the deity] upon *dharma* and the other [qualities], the knower of the ritual procedure should then apply the pedestal (*pīṭha*). The worship and the rest should be performed as previously enjoined with the *praṇava*.
The *praṇava* should be known as pertaining to all deities because it is supreme;
having meditated upon the form of the deity, whatever one conceptualizes, that shall come to be. (124)
O Six-faced One, if a Liṅga has been installed by one belonging to the quarters of Indra, Varuṇa, Kubera, or Yama in any other direction, one should perform a rite for pacification there.
That very deity is worthy of sacrifice; having performed the rites characterized by the five limbs, one should perform the oblation right there and then present a pair of cows.
Then, one should worship Śiva, the Lord of the gods and the supreme cause,
in the linga and in the fire according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Abiding in the *liṅga* or abiding in the fire, Śiva accepts the worship and the supreme oblation; assuming the form of the preceptor (*ācārya*), he bestows knowledge.
The Vidyās, Vidyeśvaras, and others should not create any distinction between the teacher, the mantra, Śivajñāna, and Śiva. (129)
The preceptor, endowed with the knowledge of Śiva and having the mantra as his very body, should always worship the Śiva-mantra, which eternally assumes all forms. || 130 ||
One should worship the Astra-mantra on the seat itself, the Gaṇeśas seated upon the bases of the world-protectors, and the Liṅga in the center, according to the proper sequence.
Having worshipped those situated like a wheel above the Vidyeśvaras, who are merged within the upper and lower powers (śakti), the knower of the ritual procedure [should proceed].

One should worship the Lord Śiva, the Sovereign of the Universe, as the upward-facing Liṅga, established in power (Śaktistha), joined with the Brahma-mantras, and surrounded by the limbs of Śiva (Śivāṅgas). || 133 ||
Having washed the *liṅga* with the scripture known as the *Śivāstra*,
those obstacles which take the form of Rudras are driven away by it. (134)
Having washed the pedestal, one should then [sprinkle] it with water from the *vardhanī* vessel;
[the obstacles] are struck down by the *pāśupata* weapon, which assumes the form of the Dawn (*uṣas*).
Having thus performed the various rites for the expulsion of obstacles, the wise one should then perform the elevation of Śiva, the Supreme Self. (136)
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the ritual dismissal of the deity;
having honored him with the five Brahmans, one should offer [the oblation] to Caṇḍeśa.
The wise man should always offer the remains of the offering (nirmālya) with his right hand, reciting in sequence: "To Dhuni Caṇḍeśvara, huṃ phaṭ svāhā. (138)
O knower of mantras, having taken the great sacrificial ladle (sruva) with both hands, the wise practitioner, having made his head like a linga, should remain [in that posture]. || 139 ||
And one should never, with the thumb above the hand, threaten obstacles with the index finger; rather, one should effect their presence by means of the *liṅgamudrā*. (140)
At the time of bathing, the wise practitioner should perform the *nirodha* rite with firmness;
having thoroughly washed his hands, the mantra-master should touch the *liṅga* again and again. (141)
Then, being soiled, one should wash the body and perform the ritual bath thereafter.
Thus ends the chapter on Consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) in the *Śrī-sarvajñānottara*.
When the fragrance has faded from the mark, one should cause it to remain;
having moved it from that place, one should deposit it behind [the image]. || 1 ||
One should employ stone in a stone abode, wood in a wooden one, likewise clay in a clay one, and gemstone in a gemstone one. (2)
Having joined it with gold, along with ghee and honey,
one should carefully install it according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Thus, by that Dhatṛ, who was skilled in ritual, the best of rites was performed;
and the Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas abandoned their unholy resort.
Make that which is too high or out of proportion level; make that which is uneven even. One should make it firm and stable, and for the sake of the ritual, one must not transgress this rule.
O Six-faced One, one should not perform the piercing in an improper location;
one should leave aside a single thread toward the south or the west.
Now, in the external sequence, even a person endowed with devotion, having abandoned the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, [should lay] the thread for Īśāna at every door.
One should not move a Śiva-liṅga, whether it be well-established or poorly situated,
but rather [one should perform the rite] according to the path taught in the scriptures with oblations of ghee in due order.
One who knows the mantras should establish the liṅga with a hundred [threads] and move it with a thousand; or he may extract it with the previous thread according to the sūtra.
Here, one should purify the water with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās).
Then, having bathed the liṅga with curd, milk, and ghee, one should dry it.
With powders produced from barley and wheat, mixed with fragrant substances and astringent decoctions, and with various intoxicating barks derived from milk-exuding trees; || 11 ||
Then one should cause the *arghya* offering to be presented, joined with these [substances], along with milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, honey, blood, sesame seeds, barley, and white mustard seeds.
Then, with perfumes, flowers, incense, garments, ornaments, and various kinds of foods, edibles, drinks, and so forth, one should meditate upon the Lord as a drop (bindu). 13.
(124) Whatever substance is to be negated, one should contemplate that very thing there as consisting of the Supreme God endowed with power, O Six-faced One, sustained by me. 14.
He who is indeed that eternal God, the giver of all, the fulfiller of all desires, omniscient, omnipresent, peaceful, liberated, and free from all affliction. || 15 ||
O Six-faced One, all substances empowered with the Śakti-mantra are auspicious;
therefore, one should employ them everywhere. || 16 ||
At the location of the deity’s head, the preceptor should perform the fire-oblation for Śiva with the Śiva-mantra, numbering one thousand times.
Then, with the Brahma-mantras and the Śiva-aṅga-mantras in their respective places in due order,
one should subsequently perform the Mūrti-homa outside for half that amount.

He is traditionally remembered as one devoted to the ritual fire-offering (homa) of the forms [of the deity], together with the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras), the attendants (gaṇas), the mantras, and likewise the world-protectors (lokapālas), each in their respective places, along with the five ancillaries (pañcāṅgas). || 19 ||
Alternatively, as previously declared for all mantras,
one should always offer libations into the fire during the sacrifice to Śiva in the same manner as for Śiva himself.
O Skanda, the deities of Vyāsa are each individually [assigned] to the words;
likewise, they are joined with the five limbs as ordained by the ritual procedure of their own mantras.
Then, having worshipped Maheśāna on a liṅga, in the fire, or even on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
those mantras— consisting of that single mantra— should be meditated upon as being endowed with all their limbs.
Having worshipped thus according to the rule, he should then offer the bali-oblation to the quarters;
and having worshipped the god Caṇḍeśvara, he should fully honor his preceptor.
With perfumes, flowers, purifiers, and the like, with garments, ornaments, and vehicles, or even in a village, market town, or city, according to the extent of one's wealth. (24)
One should not practice stinginess with wealth out of a desire to acquire great merit;
rather, one attains all desires through the performance of the ritual exactly as prescribed. (25)
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and all sacred fords—
that fruit a man shall obtain multiplied ten million times by installing a liṅga.

Whoever installs a *liṅga* according to this procedure, preceded by the proper rites and accompanied by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), shall obtain merit proclaimed in all the Āgamas multiplied ten million times ten millionfold. || 27 ||
Whatever three-fold suffering arises from the side of the father or the mother,
having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, may he thereafter attain the supreme goal.
He who, out of greed, performs [a rite] without having understood the scripture according to the prescribed rules, shall destroy both the performer and himself in this world and the next. (29)
Therefore, a wise person should have [this] performed according to the rules with every effort;
both the one who performs it and the one who causes it to be performed thereby goes to the supreme goal. || 30 ||
Thus ends the chapter on the restoration of the dilapidated in the venerable Sarvajñānottara.
This procedure has been proclaimed for movable lingas and for [movable] ordinances;
now, declare accurately regarding immovable ones and images.

If a movable linga is installed by one who does not know the truth, it shall become [defective]; the rule for its [removal] and the procedure for that is traditionally recorded as being performed by an architect or someone else. || 2 ||
Whether made of gold, silver, copper, stone,
or clay, that pedestal fashioned [for it] shall render the Liṅga immovable. (3)
One should purify the water for the weapons with the five products of the cow through dhāraṇa and other rites;
one should establish it with all the seed-syllables, accompanied by the nasal bindu and the prolated vowel.
Through meditation, let the deity go to the seat along with the seed-syllable and the jewel;
she should remember her by means of the Praṇava according to the previously stated procedure.
Indra, Pāvaka, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Īśa, and Brahmānanda are the presiding deities. || 6 ||
One should arrange the elements beginning with earth and ending with smell upon the altar of Brahman;
the Supporter (Dhārikā) is to be known at the head, and one should place Dharma and the other [virtues] at the feet.
And those very bonds, functioning through qualities that exist in mutual dependence,
having formed four limbs, [operate] upon passion and so forth, as well as on the veils and so on.
Then, upon the upper surface of the sandalwood [pedestal], one should further fashion the Māyā and Vidya [tattvas];
or else, one should contemplate the Liṅga within that [space] as extending up to Śiva.
It is the radiance of the ray of purity, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns;
it is the support of all the gods and the bestower of the fruits of devotion and liberation. || 10 ||
Upon his head is a white lotus, beautiful with its lovely pericarp, which is dissolved therein.
One should always fashion the liṅga as having eight petals with beautiful filaments at their edges; it is thus pleasing to the mind. Then, one should establish Śiva therein.
And one should worship in due order according to the previously stated procedure,
with the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ, and indeed with the Vaṣaṭ-call itself.
Having worshipped them, one should indeed employ the eyes and faces;
having worshipped them, one should employ incense, foodstuffs, and so forth, in due order. (14)
For the deity stationed in the fire, salutation is offered with perfumes, flowers, and purifiers;
likewise, it is also placed upon the garments and within the vessels of the arghya offering.
O Skanda, the procedure for all lingas has been briefly stated by me.
Now learn from me how it should be performed with diligence regarding images.
One should have an image made— endowed with the primary marks, whether it be a painted relief or otherwise—
in a form exactly corresponding to the appearance of the deity.
One should perform the bath as before with water consecrated by mantras, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and so forth;
likewise, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūta-śuddhi) through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās).
O Six-faced One, having established the deity with the first [mantra] in a gentle manner,
one should then assign the limbs, as well as the eyes and the faces.
Having intentionally visualized the form of the deity as pure as the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, with a serene countenance, gentle, and adorned with all ornaments. (20)
One should offer perfumes, flowers, garments, ornaments, incense, sacrificial materials, and lamps with one's own heart-mantra. (21)
Bathing is always prescribed in all types of ponds—those made of jewels, silver, and copper, as well as those made of stone. || 22 ||
One should have paintings and plastered images of him made by physicians;
and one should recollect him with the mantra of the Omniscient One while offering water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering. (23)
Having performed the placement of mantras (vinyāsa) solely with flowers and without water,
one should offer incense and provide an offering of food (naivedya). (24)
One should perfume that house with fragrant flowers and incense;
furthermore, one should create a splendor of garments with excellent cloths of variegated colors. (25)
Having fashioned it with arches, banners, umbrellas, and beautiful, auspicious flags, and with various artistic arrangements, one should install the deities.
Then, with his senses restrained, he should first perform the fire sacrifice (homa) for the deity who has been installed, using her mantras as before.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in front of all the installed deities;
for the constant performance of fire-rites, there should be a separate chamber.
* * * * * * * * for each deity in the Pratisthā [section].
Thus ends the chapter on images and so forth in the Sarvajñānottara.
Furthermore, I shall again proclaim the determination of the rules for recitation (japa), and how one attains the proper time for its intensification and dismissal. || 1 ||

From the recitation, the fire-offering (homa) should be one-tenth; at the conclusion of the recitation, ten lakhs [of oblations] are prescribed, O child—ten million for the highest accomplishment in the practice of attaining success.
For the middle [size], however, there are five faces; for the smallest, twenty-five. One should perform all minor rites with half that [number]. || 3 ||
Trees with long thorns, such as the nimba, tinduka, vibhītaka,
aśvakarṇa, and śleṣmātaka, are to be known as suitable for rites of a cruel nature.
(129) Those that are double-tipped, split, crooked, with crooked cuts,
or intensely blazing— such poisonous lac-dyes should be employed in cruel rites.
O Skanda, those [staves] produced from milk-trees, which were mentioned as being otherwise [than the previously described],
are to be understood as suitable for rites of pacification (śāntikarma), with the exception of those born from the Brahma-tree.

Those creepers situated amidst tender shoots, free from knots, with smooth bark, devoid of disease, and without wounds— these are considered auspicious for both peaceful and fierce rites when their fibers run in the reverse direction.
O Six-faced One, uneven sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should always be understood as intended for cruel rites; those that are even are for rites of pacification, attraction, and nourishment.
Through constant fire-offerings (homa), she brings about fortune and the accomplishment of goals;
through recitation (japa), she effects the purification of sins; and through knowledge and meditation, one is liberated.
The assembly of distinguished people, the salutation of royal persons, and the power of self-exaltation—if these exist, success is certain. (10)
One perceives signs of accomplishment pertaining to the divine, the atmospheric, and the terrestrial;
or else, having heard a voice within, one should collect the auspicious materials.
Metals such as puṣpaloha and others, mercury and the secondary minerals (uparasas), upavīta, añjana and the rest, realgar, and manahśilā; || 12 ||

One should pierce iron that has been struck by the group of enemies with ghee and honey; having processed it in the juice of the *prahi* plant and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should fashion the excellent weapon.
One should purify mercury and secondary minerals by heating them in a crucible;
the purification of iron and other metals prior to the homa and other rites has been previously enjoined.
(130) Whatever substance is proclaimed in the Root Tantras as the means for purifying this [substance], one should not purify that very same thing further in the Rasa Tantra. 15.
One should perform the touching of the ritual substances according to the rules for the rosary;
O child, the threefold means of accomplishing the substances has been explained as it was told of old.
It is traditionally taught as being superior, middling, and inferior respectively, and as being characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), and darkness (tāmasa). || 17 ||
One should know that which is blazing to be sāttvika; that which has smoke is declared to be rājasa;
and one who is discerning should know that which is hot to be tāmasa. (8)
"Rising up, the celestial nymphs are seen with blazing fire accompanied by smoke; they appear as if possessed of heat—thus there are these three states. (19)
Then, the knower of the ritual procedure should visualize the seed-mantra, himself,
and his own form as being situated within the point (bindu) and presided over by Śakti.
Mercury [is the antidote] for mercury, disease for disease, a courtesan for a courtesan, and sandals for sandals; in this way, orpiment and realgar are likewise neutralized.
O Six-faced One, when that which consists of *bindu* and *nāda* becomes audible through the ear, then it swiftly accomplishes all undertakings; not otherwise.
White is to be known for pacifying rites, yellow for rites of nourishment;
like a peacock [in color] it is prescribed for killing, and it is remembered as being used for driving away [enemies]. (23)
Resembling the peak of Mount Indrakopa, it is used for the rite of subjugation;
for causing enmity, one should employ that which is smoke-colored and of the nature of wind.
Having a form like a rainbow, and likewise focused on drawing [the breath] inward,
the Bindu is known to consist of all colors and to perform all actions. (25)
And he who, by means of the six-fold covering, beholds that which resides between the eyebrows, resembling pure crystal, by means of the instrument [of yoga]. || 26 ||
The exhalation and inhalation of embodied beings, residing within their bodies through the practice of yoga, become the risen sun and the moon consisting of its sixteen digits. (27)
That very time is without beginning or end, in which everything is established;
it enters into that again, and from that alone it proceeds.
In the south, the movement of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti) reveals the self to embodied beings;
likewise, by means of the north, it reveals the Lord (Īśvara) here once again.
The three-year [period] is to be known from the two great ones; the two-year [period] from the three; likewise, the one-year [period] for the sake of the day by means of the six.
When the sun moves in the northern course, then tell me again of the death occurring within a day and night for embodied beings. || 31 ||
Having seen death in this manner, if one desires to live,
then, O gentle one, he should contemplate that very Lord who dwells within him.

O Guha, within that [lotus], one should perceive oneself as consisting of that [light], having the luster of a pure jasmine flower or the moon, possessing the radiance of a conch shell or cow’s milk, and having the form of nectar.
Furthermore, whether preceded by a vowel or not, these are proclaimed as the Immortals (amṛta).
One should constantly retain that very [mantra], and one shall not fall under the power of death. || 34 ||
One should offer oblations of *dūrvā* grass smeared with the three sweets, or likewise two finger-breadths of *amṛtā*;
or one may offer them smeared with the three sweets while reciting [the mantra] with the *pluta* (protracted) vowel. || 35 ||
Then, having become disenchanted with this long-lasting and unstable life, one should contemplate the god who is time itself and whose form is death. (36)
The form, pierced by fire and situated in the center of the *suṣumnā*,
resembles a blazing flame and is adorned with crests of radiant light.
Drawing up [the vital breath] with sound to the crown of the head, one should bring the life-breaths to a state of equilibrium;
having concentrated the mind upon Kālājū, one whose senses are motionless should remain in meditative absorption (samādhi). 38.
Having properly brought about the two pulsations and indeed all the gates,
they should be struck at the head with the force of the wind by means of the kṣurikā weapon.
One engaged in the cultivation of the letter A should meditate on that which consists of the bindu and nāda;
thus one is liberated from the vital breaths in that very [state] which has been proclaimed. 40.
Everything, whether gross or subtle, arises from the Bindu and Nāda;
therefore, one should worship the Bindu, which is the essence of Śakti.
But just as one who is endowed with a pure mind should remain established in that state, so too,
when devoid of wealth, he should wander for alms, [accepting] even broken grains and not seeking fine food.
Thus ends the chapter on the means of attaining supernatural powers and the practitioner thereof in the Sarvajñānottara.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the sequential procedure for the practice of alms-gathering,
as well as eating, sleeping, purification, postures, and the basis of recitation.
The wise one should always hold the vessel with the *hṛd* mantra; having washed it with the *astra* seed-syllable, he should encircle it with the *kavaca* mantra. (2)
Meditating on Īśāna in the center, the knower of mantras should likewise contemplate the Gāyatrī weapon;
being pure, he should always go for alms while reciting the Astra mantra.
Having placed the Astra-mantra upon his staff and the Gāyatrī itself upon his umbrella,
he should then daily wander for alms, avoiding those who are outcasted or censured.
Having returned, he should again place that vessel in the purification area;
then, having taken up the image once more, he should perform the cleansing of the legs.
Having sipped water and sprinkled himself, being purified in soul, he should sprinkle the sacrificial oblation (caru) again;
having cleansed it according to the rule, he should place it within the self of the deity and the fire.
Then, having offered the *prāṇāhuti* oblations and performed the *śivahoma* again in due order,
one should eat a small amount of smooth food at night when it has become cool.
Having sipped water and gone outside, he should likewise eat this forest-fruit;
then, having smeared [the body] and sipped water again, he should proceed according to the prescribed rule.
On a pure and clean patch of ground dug three cubits deep,
having once again prepared a dwelling for recitation that is complete with all auspicious characteristics, [one should sit] upon the surface of the earth.
It was provided with canopies and banners, adorned with the beauty of flags,
and decorated with various artistic works depicting the sports and other activities of the incarnations of Rudra.
A wise person should always construct a bed measuring nine, eleven, or even seven cubits, according to the previously mentioned ritual manual.
The knower of mantras, having secured the armor with a five-colored thread,
should wrap it three times starting from the region of the door.

Standing at a distance of one cubit (*ratni*), having worshipped in due order the two *kīlas* together with the deities of the directions, and the *aṅgas* placed in their respective positions, [one should proceed]. (13)
One should place four full jars in the intermediate directions;
one should worship Rudra in the abode of Śiva, either with the [appropriate] mantra or through meditation, O Guha.
Resembling a wind of blazing splendor, formidable and terrifying with its fangs, with hands raised holding weapons, it is fierce and the destroyer of all obstacles. || 15 ||
Then one should place the Śakti on the ground and place the Vidyā above it;
thereafter, one should apply the wheel of vowels and the phonemes in their proper sequence.
As before, the body [should be protected] with the mantra-fortress and weapons;
then the yogi, with a tranquil mind, should lie down and behold Śiva with equanimity.
Constantly reciting that very mantra while relying on meditation, the knower of mantras should likewise perform worship at the midnight libation.
Likewise, one should perform the lying down and, upon waking, the recitation;
having understood the movement of the deity, one should perform the recitation, meditation, and so forth in their proper sequence. (19)
Then, having risen at the half-watch [of the night] and meditated upon the god who wields the Pināka bow,
he should mentally recite that Praṇava devoid of the Bindu.
Having emerged from the place of rest, perform the necessary bodily functions;
wearing the sacred thread externally, with your gaze directed outward, proceed step by step.

During the day one should stand facing the north; at night, the student indeed faces the south; at midnight, however, he faces the southwest; and during the two twilights, he faces as he does during the day.
O Six-faced One, having meditated upon wood, grass, stone, or a clod of earth as vomit,
one should then perform the purification of impurity while covered by a cloth. (23)
One should not do so in rivers, nor on ashes, nor on cow dung;
nor in a thicket, nor on a grassy meadow, nor near the temples of Praśamīśa or Upavana.
O Guha, having touched your anus with a piece of wood or a clod of earth,
and having grasped your penis, perform the ritual of applying earth.
One should avoid sand and saline soil, as well as the earth from the roots of trees, from anthills, and likewise that which has been used for village paths. (26)
Having taken pure clay, one should place it on the bank of a river;
then, taking clay and water, one should perform purification.
Three applications of clay are prescribed for the penis, seven for the anus, and ten for one hand;
seventy are prescribed for both hands by one desiring purification with clay.
In each interval, three purifications shall be performed;
then the practitioner of mantra should consume the consecrated tooth-stick.
Having sipped water according to the rule and having risen, one should again scatter [the ashes] in sequence;
thereafter, one should perform meditation until the sun has risen.
Then one should perform a bath once in flowing water;
thereafter, for the fulfillment of all desires, there is the bath with sacred ash.
"The Varuṇa [mantra] is proclaimed for the destruction of stains and odors.
Thus ends the section on the practice of begging for alms and so forth in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*.
136) Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme Vāruṇa bath, O Skanda; it is the highest purifier, which destroys [bodily] smears and odors. || 1 ||
Having first washed his hands and feet, taken earth from the riverbank,
and sipped water to become pure, he should meditate upon the stainless Śiva.
One should perform the sprinkling with the Astra mantra; take up the earth. Having consecrated it with the Astra-bīja, one should collect it with the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having placed it on the bank of the water and washed it at the water's edge,
one should first wash it with the Astra-mantra and then establish it with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
They should not sprinkle [water] again; from that, one should divide it once more into three parts:
in the southeast, as well as in the north.
First, the Astra-mantra should be recited; the Brahma-mantra on the right;
and the Śiva-mantra on the left—one should perform each separately.
One should cast the consecrated weapon-mantra (astra) into all ten directions in due order;
then, by means of the application of the iron-arrow weapon (nārācāstra), one should cast it again into the midst of the water.
Having meditated upon the fiery concentration (āgneyī dhāraṇā), one should again contemplate the nectar;
then, with a portion consecrated by the recitation of the Śiva-mantra, one should cause it to return into the water.
O Six-faced One, by this procedure, Śivatīrtha indeed comes into being.
Here ends the section.
Having washed the feet of the one whose feet are above all knowledge (*Sarvajñānottara*)— that is, the shanks, the feet, and likewise the hands— again and again;
Having recited [the mantra], one should then bathe in the midst of the Śivatīrtha.

With the ritual honors due to a universal monarch, using fragrant *āmalaka* fruits and other substances, with the limbs of Brahmā, with the *Śivagāyatrī*, and with the great weapon-mantra of Śiva; || 2 ||
One who knows the ritual procedure should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) as well as the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana),
having withdrawn all mantras by means of the resonant sound (nināda).
Having drawn [the deity] forth, one should establish it within one's own heart by means of the path of emergence;
thereafter, the wise practitioner, with flowers in hand, should proceed to the sanctuary.
But when one is unable to perform the Varuṇa bath due to illness or other reasons,
then, having washed one's hands and feet, one should perform the ash bath (bhasmasnāna).
Thus ends the section on the Varuṇa-bath in the venerable Sarvajñānottara.
I shall describe the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) in brief and not in detail;
it is a supreme, meritorious rite that destroys all sins and is the pinnacle of all knowledge.
Taking cow dung situated in the sky or fallen in an auspicious place,
one should discard the lower portion and grind it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
In a secluded, uninhabited, and delightful place, free from all disturbances,
devoid of mud and anthills, and well-ventilated, one should dry it thoroughly.
The wise one should collect the dry [materials] and sprinkle them with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra-bīja);
then, having generated the fire of Śiva, he should burn [the impurities] with that fire.
Then, in brief, O Skanda, one should again burn the forest cow-dung combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the prescribed ritual.
If even that is not available, one should burn again in this same manner something that is free from the scent of ash and smearing, situated in a clean place, and pure. (11)
Having withdrawn [the deity] into his heart with the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should place [the substance] in a new vessel while reciting the Astra-mantra, which destroys all obstacles.
Having consecrated water with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the ritual bath for removing impurities;
thereafter, the knower of mantras should perform the formal bath (vidhisnāna), beginning from the head.
O Six-faced One, O Śiva, one should not perform the consecration with the external Brahma-mantras in their successive order until the very end.
Having dusted himself off according to the rule, the wise man should put on his loincloth;
then, having washed his feet and hands with earth, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) once more. 15.
The knower of the mantra should drink water consecrated with the three truths three times;
he should then wipe his mouth three times according to the sequence, as far as his ability permits.
Then, with the syllable Om (praṇava), the wise one should touch the tuft of hair, the eyes, and so forth;
having sipped water again according to the rule, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Having always performed the salutation at the junctions of the day with all the mantras,
the wise one should then practice meditation and perform the threefold recitation.
One should daily recite the three groups of six meritorious [mantras] through the actions of mind, speech, and body,
in the morning, at midday, and likewise in the evening, following the sequence beginning with the temple.
Or, having meditated upon Śiva in all things, one should constantly remember Him during recitations and meditations;
by restraining the activity of the vital breaths, one shall not incur any sin.
Or, the knower of mantras should constantly recite the *saṃhitā* three times a day,
one hundred and eight syllables for the purification of all sins. (21)
For the sake of destroying all obstacles and indeed the net of snares,
one should constantly brandish weapons of terrible form.
Having thus become composed of mantra, one should employ all mantras;
the yogi should contemplate the Rudra-mantras and the qualities consisting of yoga.
The Chapter on the Ash-Bath in the Śrī-Sarvajñānottara.
Hereafter I shall explain [the practice of] always carrying a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). || 25 ||
O Lord of Yogins, he who was without a companion had a friend who, knowing the ritual procedures, carried a water-pot and a blazing fire with a terrible weapon.
Having risen in the morning, one should daily purify that water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) on the body with copper ash,
and likewise purify the water within it with ashes.
Having thoroughly purified silver and gold that are covered with stains, impurities, and smells,
one should thereafter fill them with water filtered through a cloth.
One should constantly perform the rites of water for the feet, sipping water, and purification in their proper sequence;
one should not touch anything until both hands are dry. (29)
With hands thoroughly dried and his self purified, he performed the prescribed duties;
he used no garment, bed, or water-pot that had been used by another.
One should never smear oneself with ashes on auspicious lunar days; nor should one share one's own bed, one's own garment, one's wife, one's children, or one's water-pot [with others]. (31)
(140) These things are pure for oneself, but would be impure for others.
This is the section on the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) from the *Śrīsarvajñānottara*.
Thus ends the Sarvajñānottarapāda.
